`t3_thread_launch` is the single-thread launch tool. Use `create_threads` only for a batch of threads intentionally sharing the caller's checkout: it always inherits the caller's project, branch, and worktree and has no workspace override. Asking an agent to run `git worktree add` or `cd` in its prompt does not update T3's thread binding. Select the workspace in the launch call instead. `t3_worktree_handoff` moves the calling thread, not another thread, and cannot move a thread already attached to a worktree.

`t3_thread_launch` has no idempotency key. Retain its returned threadId and inspect it with `t3_thread_read` / `t3_thread_wait`; preparation can still be running after acceptance. If a launch fails or its response is lost, inspect `t3_thread_list` before retrying, since a thread may already exist.

Tool names may include a harness-normalized MCP prefix, such as `mcp__t3_code__delegate_task`; the semantics are the same. Some harnesses attach optional MCP servers lazily: if an initial tool-catalog scan does not show T3 tools, do not conclude that cross-provider delegation is unavailable. Make one bounded direct attempt using the known T3 tool name on the next tool step. In Codex code mode, for example, call `tools.mcp__t3_code__orchestrator_capabilities({})` before reporting that the capability is absent. Keep polling/wait loops bounded, do not duplicate active work, and use stable `clientRequestId` values when retrying tools that accept them.

ACP fallback: some ACP agents accept the injected MCP server but fail to expose its tools. When the T3 tools are absent and `T3_ACP_MCP_NODE` is present, call the same tools through the terminal: `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$T3_ACP_MCP_NODE" ${T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT:+"$T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT"} acp-mcp-call orchestrator_capabilities '{}'` (`T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT` is unset when T3 runs as a standalone executable). Delegate with `acp-mcp-call delegate_task '{"task":"...","target":{"providerInstanceId":"...","model":"..."},"mode":"async","clientRequestId":"..."}'`. This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

- When model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty `inheritedOptions` from `orchestrator_capabilities`, use `delegate_task` even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Read the selected model's descriptors from `orchestrator_capabilities` and put settings in `target.options`, not only in the prompt. Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.


### Background work you wait on

Before you end your turn to wait for a background command or Monitor you started, such as tests, a build, or a CI wait, call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID. The thread then stays in the user's Working list until that task ends, instead of returning to them early. Do not mark a dev server, a watcher, or anything else you leave running.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__delegate_task
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Delegate one task to a T3-owned child agent/subagent of THIS thread and run it with only the supplied task prompt, without copying parent conversation history. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use t3_thread_send on its childThreadId. Set isolation to worktree for a separate checkout based on the parent local commit, with project setup completed before the child starts. Uncommitted edits are not copied; omitted isolation shares the parent checkout. Use delegate_task when model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty inheritedOptions from orchestrator_capabilities, even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Set target.options using advertised IDs: Claude {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Check providerInstanceId, model, and options in the result. Provider/model and modes inherit unless overridden. Options inherit only for the same instance and model; explicit entries override individual values and [] or {} clears them. A requested runtimeMode must be one the target provider lists in orchestrator_capabilities runtimeModes; an inherited one steps down to the broadest mode it offers. Leave runtimeMode unset unless the user asks for a supervised child: approval-required and auto-accept-edits usually make the child wait for a person at each action that needs approval. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion, a blocking question, a pending approval, or timeout. If hasPendingQuestion, pass threadId=childThreadId to t3_pending_request_list, t3_pending_request_read (with requestId) and t3_pending_request_respond, or ask the user; the task's completion still wakes this thread. If pendingApproval is set, read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback. It grants no approval authority; decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder, and pending request tools answer questions only. The child keeps running and its completion still wakes this thread. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

anyOf.description: Model options from orchestrator_capabilities. For the same provider instance and model, overrides individual inherited values; [] or {} clears them. Claude: {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex: {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Only use options advertised by the selected model.
Defaults to shared: use the parent's checkout. Worktree creates a separate checkout from the parent's current local commit before starting the child. Uncommitted edits are not copied.

Defaults to async. Use wait only when this turn needs the child's result before you can continue. A blocking question or a pending approval in the child ends the wait early with the task still running.

timeoutMs.description: Wait budget for mode=wait only. Default 10 minutes. Elapsing it returns waitTimedOut=true on that call and does not cancel the child.

anyOf.description: Defaults to inherit; omit it unless the user asks for a supervised child. A narrower mode is not a read-only switch: on most providers, approval-required and auto-accept-edits pause the child at each action that needs approval until a person approves it in the child's thread, which this thread cannot do. To limit what the child does, say so in the task. A mode ranked above this thread's is rejected; that ranking does not promise the child's provider permissions are narrower than this thread's.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__orchestrator_capabilities
tools.description: List the V2 provider instances, a short list of their models from the same live catalog as the composer, inherited runtime settings, and app-owned orchestration features available to this caller. The list has the user's favorite and custom models, your own model, every current Codex, Claude, Muse and Grok model, and the first 8 current models of other providers. Other legacy models are left out. omittedModels counts models left out; pass search, such as 'sonnet 4.6', to find them. delegate_task accepts any catalog model, listed or not. For a separate top-level thread in a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_background_wait
tools.description: Keep this thread in the user's Working list and out of their inbox while you wait for background work. Start a background command or Monitor first. Call this before you end your turn if you will act on its result when it wakes you. In taskIds, give the ID shown when the task started. The thread stays in Working until the task ends. The user is not told the work is done. Do not mark work you leave running, such as a dev server or watcher. Unmarked commands and monitors never keep the thread in Working. Pass waiting=false to remove the mark. This does not stop the task. IDs that are not running return in unmatched and change nothing. Only Claude threads support this tool. Other providers return an error.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_send
tools.description: Send a message to any T3 thread in this environment. The target cannot have broader permission modes than the caller. Use delegate_task with the full review context and a new clientRequestId for independent review rounds. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, send to its childThreadId. After the original task completes, a requested follow-up creates a fresh task in that child thread and returns taskId when it starts a turn or restarts a turn without its own task; its completion notifies the parent, and the original result stays unchanged. A steer that joins a running turn returns that turn's task, if it has one. mode='auto' starts an idle thread, steers a fully active turn, or queues behind a turn that is not yet steerable. Use queue for a separate follow-up turn, steer for an in-flight update, or restart to interrupt-and-restart the active turn. clientRequestId makes retries idempotent.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__task_status
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Read a T3-owned delegated task created by this parent thread. childRunId identifies the original delegated run. workState distinguishes working, waiting_for_children, and result_available; a completed turn with live nested work is not a completed task. summary is the final task result, including provider errors on failure, and remains stable after publication. hasPendingChildRuns reports later queued or executing turns in the backing child thread, even after the task is terminal; it does not reopen the task, and task_cancel stops those turns too. Turns held in a stopped queue wait for the user and do not count. latestTerminal* provides later non-monitor turn results; latestTerminalSummary and latestTerminalResultContextTransferId are independently null when they exactly repeat summary and resultContextTransferId, respectively. pendingApproval identifies the oldest pending live approval for this task's own unfinished work. Read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback and grants no approval authority. Decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder. Reading a terminal result acknowledges its automatic parent delivery.

input.message:
Thanks for being straight about it. Please carry on and finish the lane. Here's how to make it tractable:

1. **Do the transport first and commit it on its own.** `LoopbackClient::send_completion` / `stream_completion` over `std::net::TcpStream`, plus the coordinator wiring, plus hermetic `TcpListener` tests. That's the smaller, self-contained half. Commit once its tests and clippy pass.

2. **Then do the LiteRT lifecycle, as a second commit.** "Good enough" for cancellation and bounds means:
   - Each subprocess phase (`list`, `import`, `serve` readiness) has a deadline. Enforce it with a `try_wait()` poll loop plus `kill()`/`wait()` when the deadline passes.
   - Read `list` stdout on a helper thread into a buffer capped at `MAX_REGISTRY_OUTPUT_BYTES`. Drain and discard anything beyond the cap so the child can't block on a full pipe. Then join the thread.
   - Readiness and startup accept an optional `CancellationToken` (or an `Arc<AtomicBool>`), checked on every 150ms poll.
   - Every failure path, a cancel, `stop()` and `Drop` must kill and reap the child.
   - Process-group / descendant cleanup isn't required. Note it as a known limit.
   That's sufficient. Don't hold out for more.

3. **Compiling:** the first `cargo test` build is slow; that's expected. Run it with a generous timeout, or in the background and wait for it. Don't stop it partway. `--no-default-features` skips gpui and typst, so it should be manageable. If the slow part is a genuine compile error, fix it rather than abandoning the work.

4. **If you run out of road on the lifecycle,** commit the transport anyway. Report exactly what remains and why. One real half beats nothing.

The original brief still applies for everything else: file ownership, test commands, the final report format, and the PORT_PLAN replacement text.

# Nix's ALSA cannot load the host's PipeWire plugin (it needs host libraries),

content.text:
Lane B (audio devices) is done, and real playback and microphone capture now work on this machine. All 4 audio checks pass, including both hardware checks, and so do the 18 existing audio contract checks.

Terra's hardware checks failed at first, but the backend code wasn't at fault. The dev shell was loading Fedora's PipeWire audio plugin, which depends on libraries the Nix shell can't load, so no device would open. I pointed `devenv.nix` at a PipeWire plugin built by Nix instead (commit `34b7b7b4`, on top of Terra's `78b8073b`).

Things that are still open for this lane:
- **Other platforms:** macOS and Windows builds haven't been tried.
- **Sample formats:** the backend handles the common device formats (i16, u16, f32). Anything else reports "format unsupported".
- **Strict Clippy:** with warnings treated as errors, Clippy still fails on dead code in `editor/block_moves.rs` and `margin_rail_view.rs`. That code was already there before this lane and only shows up with the `--no-default-features` build. It passes once dead-code warnings are allowed. I'll check whether it also shows up in the merged full build.

Lane A (local AI, second attempt) and lane C (AI settings) are still running. When both are in, I'll merge all three branches and check the combined build.

Summarise: what it speeds up (Rust/cargo builds? linker? caching?), how it is installed and invoked, requirements (OS, Nix, rustc version), whether it works as a drop-in for cargo build/test/clippy, remote/shared caching, maturity/stars/release status, license, and any benchmark numbers. Quote exact install/usage commands.

content.content:
# blaze: summary

**What it is:** A tool for fast **incremental Rust compilation**. It isn't primarily a cache or a linker replacement. Per the README, it "keeps your project compiled in memory," recompiles only the functions you edited, and patches them into the existing binary "instead of linking it again from scratch." It also supports **hot reload**: programs that opt in can take new code while running. It is built on rust-analyzer (its analysis and MIR), Cranelift, LLVM/inkwell for optimised tiers, and salsa.

**Install:**
```
curl -fsSL https://ix.dev/blaze | sh
```
crates.io and Nix are also supported (see `docs/install.md`). On first use it downloads its own Rust (about 125–160 MB) or uses rustup's.

**Usage:** You run your usual cargo commands with `blaze` in front:
```
blaze run     # like cargo run
blaze test    # like cargo test
blaze build   # like cargo build
```
The README says `fmt`, `clippy`, `doc`, `tree` and other commands are blaze's own and "run no cargo." A rebuilt binary is marked by `[blaze]` in the `Finished` line. There's also a demo: `nix run github:indexable-inc/blaze#life`.

**Drop-in for cargo?** Mostly, but with caveats:
- It mirrors cargo's commands, and a doc covers making plain `cargo build` use blaze.
- The authors say to "Keep `cargo check` or your CI as the final word."
- The README is a bit inconsistent. It says blaze "runs beside cargo" and patches the program cargo built, but also that the first build uses "no cargo build and no rustc."
- Some lines look garbled by a rename, e.g. "`blaze run` is the same as `blaze run`."

**Requirements:**
- **OS:** macOS on Apple silicon and Linux (x86-64 and aarch64). Windows x86-64 (MSVC) works when run by hand, but isn't tested in CI and has no installer or sandbox.
- **Rust version:** blaze always uses its own toolchain, `blaze-2026-10-27` (currently that date's nightly), regardless of what your project pins. Both stable and `#![feature(...)]` code build.
- **Nix:** optional, except for the demo.
- **Memory:** "a few GB for a small project."

**Remote/shared caching:** The README doesn't document it. The repo has a `worker/remote-cache` directory, and the team is working with some companies on "fast Rust CI and remote builds" with early access. CI runner and roadmap docs exist.

**Maturity:** The README says "It's young." The repo has about 1.6k stars, 50 forks, 3 watchers, 3,305 commits, 93 open issues and 20 PRs. No releases appear on the page.

**License:** MIT or Apache-2.0, your choice.

**Benchmarks (edit-rebuild vs `cargo build`):**
- Average speedups: 10× on macOS arm64, 24× on Linux aarch64, 11× on Linux x86-64.
- About 20 ms from saving a file to the running program using the new code, with live edits.

Edit one function, then build (Linux x86-64):

| Project | cargo build | blaze build | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| ripgrep | 508 ms | 56 ms | 9.1× |
| nushell | 1.25 s | 236 ms | 5.3× |
| helix | 2.15 s | 116 ms | 19× |
| bun (1.25M lines) | 9.11 s | 451 ms | 20× |

The headline "up to 92x faster" isn't backed by any number shown on this page; the full data is in `docs/benchmarks.md`.

content.thinking:
I'm weighing whether this fits our GPUI desktop port: our real bottleneck is cold builds of gpui+typst in fresh worktrees, which this tool doesn't speed up since it mainly helps incremental rebuilds and needs its own initial build, plus remote caching is still early access. There's also a toolchain mismatch since it forces its own nightly rather than our devenv-pinned Rust with clangLinker.

For the worktree swarm, the bigger win would probably come from sccache or sharing CARGO_TARGET_DIR rather than this tool, since the lanes' real pain is cold compiles, not edit-rebuild loops — though concurrent cargo processes sharing a target dir would just serialize via lock anyway.

Where it might genuinely help is the interactive GPUI dev loop itself — hot-reloading UI changes in ~20ms would be great for visual parity iteration and capture loops. I'm hesitant about actually trying it though, since installing via curl|sh runs a remote script; I'd rather consider a sandboxed trial or ask the user first rather than install directly onto the machine.

content.text:
I read the README. Blaze would help the desktop port, but in a different place than our slow builds.

**What it does:** blaze keeps the project compiled in memory. When you edit a function, it recompiles only that function and patches it into the existing binary instead of relinking. Programs that opt in can also take the new code while running. Its benchmarks show 5–20× faster edit-then-rebuild than `cargo build` on large projects, and about 20 ms from saving to running code.

**Where it would help us:** the visual parity work. Most of the remaining port is adjusting spacing, wrapping and layout, then recapturing at 1280×860. Going from a rebuild and relaunch to about 20 ms per change would make that loop much faster.

**Where it wouldn't:**
- **Today's slow builds were cold first builds.** Each Terra lane compiled gpui and typst from scratch in a fresh worktree. blaze speeds up rebuilds after an edit, not first builds. The shared cache that would help is early-access only.
- **Our own checks wouldn't run through it.** blaze brings its own nightly Rust (`blaze-2026-10-27`) whatever we pin, and runs its own `clippy`. Our gates are devenv's pinned Rust with the clang linker and strict `cargo clippy`, and the authors themselves say to keep cargo or CI as the final word. So it would sit next to devenv as a dev tool, not replace the build.
- **It's young.** There are no releases, Windows is untested, and parts of the README are garbled.
- **Unknown risk.** Our vendored gpui crates, build scripts and `[patch.crates-io]` setup are exactly what could trip it up. Only a trial will tell.

For the slow swarm builds specifically, a compiler cache shared by all worktrees (sccache, set up in `devenv.nix`) would fix the cold-build problem and keep our pinned Rust. That's my suggestion, not something from blaze's README.

**What I'd suggest:** once the merged-branch build finishes, try blaze through `nix run` rather than its `curl | sh` installer, so nothing gets installed. I'd time it on one native UI edit compared with cargo, and check that the app starts. If it handles our setup, I'd add it as an optional dev command next to `desktop.gpui`. Do you want me to run that trial, and also add the shared compiler cache?

# blaze: Nix, toolchain, cargo support, and limitations (from `docs/install.md`)

## Nix

**Install into your profile:**
```
nix profile install github:indexable-inc/blaze
```

**Run without installing.** Run this inside a project; it behaves like `blaze build`:
```
nix run github:indexable-inc/blaze -- build
```

**Use as a flake input:**
```
inputs.blaze.url = "github:indexable-inc/blaze";
```
Then use `blaze.packages.${system}.default` "in a dev shell or a profile." This is the only flake output the page names.

**Binary cache:** there is none, so there is no substituter to add. The page says "Nix compiles blaze from source; there is no binary cache yet."

**Your devenv setup:** the page doesn't cover devenv. The flake input above is the only documented integration route.

## Toolchain download and using an existing nightly

- You don't need Rust or rustup. blaze ships its own toolchain, currently `blaze-2026-10-25`, which is "`rustc 1.101.0-nightly (12433c307 2026-10-24)`".
- It downloads rustc, cargo, std and std source into `~/.blaze` once. That's about 97 MB on macOS and 118–133 MB on Linux.
- The only documented way to use an existing toolchain is rustup. blaze "uses rustup's `nightly-2026-10-25` when rustup has it." To get it:
  ```
  rustup toolchain install nightly-2026-10-25
  ```
- No option for pointing at an arbitrary rustc is documented. Your devenv `languages.rust` toolchain likely won't be used.
- blaze always builds with its pinned nightly, whatever `rust-toolchain.toml` says.
- Code that nightly can't build fails "with rustc's error and a note saying which toolchain built it."
- The installer flag `--no-toolchain` delays the download until the first build.

## Cargo flags and features

- The page doesn't cover `--manifest-path`, `--features`, `--no-default-features`, `-p`, workspaces, or path/patch dependencies. It points to `usage.md` and `cargo.md` for those.
- **Build scripts and proc macros** run sandboxed, using Linux namespaces or Landlock (Linux 5.13+). Setting `BLAZE_SANDBOX=off` runs them unsandboxed, like cargo does.
- Linux installer builds include `blaze-proc-macro-srv`. The crates.io build lacks it.
- The only commands shown are `blaze run` and `blaze build`.

## Known limitations

- **Platforms:** macOS on Apple silicon, and Linux on x86-64/ARM64. Intel Macs are unsupported.
- **Windows:** there's no release build, and the installer refuses it. Install from crates.io instead. There's no sandbox, so you need `BLAZE_SANDBOX=off` for build scripts and proc macros.
- **Linux libc:** glibc 2.34+ is required. Alpine and other musl systems are unsupported.
- **Linker:** a C compiler is required for linking.
- **Containers:** if seccomp blocks both sandbox methods, use `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` or `BLAZE_SANDBOX=off`.
- **Memory:** the background process holds a few GB for small projects and "tens of GB for the largest".
- **Old names:** names from before 2026-10-28 no longer work. See `rename.md`.

## Other install routes

```
curl -fsSL https://ix.dev/blaze | sh
cargo +nightly-2026-10-25 install --locked blaze-engine
cargo binstall blaze-engine
```

# blaze (`docs/cargo.md`): what is supported, what falls back to cargo, what isn't supported

## Supported on the daemon path

- **Flags the doc lists:** "`--target` naming the host, a single `-p`, `--features`, `--bin`, `--example`, `--test`, `--lib`, `--manifest-path`," and also "`--workspace`, `--no-run`, `--no-fail-fast`, `-q`, test filters and the arguments after `--`".
- **`blaze test` targets:** it builds what cargo would test, or just "what `--lib`, `--bin`, `--example` and one `--test` name."
- **Harness flags kept in the test cache:** `-q`, `--nocapture`, `--show-output`, `--test-threads` and `--color`.
- **`blaze check` is broader:** "A check takes `--message-format` (each of cargo's values), `-Z`, `--exclude` and several `--target`s". It also accepts `--lib`, `--bins`, `--tests`, `--examples`, `--benches` and `--all-targets`.
- **Build scripts** are supported, but they always run sandboxed. Their environment is filtered: "what else the shell had is not there". You can add variables with `build-script-env`.
  - Their output is checked. For example, "a `rustc-link-arg` is one of a short list (`-pthread`, `-rdynamic`, `-Wl,--as-needed`, ...".
  - They may forward `CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS`.
- **Proc macros:** "By default every proc macro of a load is built by blaze, from its source, as a WebAssembly module". The escape hatches are `native-proc-macros` or `BLAZE_PROC_MACRO_WASM=0`.
- **cdylib libraries** are linked, and they honor `cargo:rustc-link-arg` and `cargo:rustc-cdylib-link-arg`.
- **Profiles:** blaze reads "the `[profile]` tables of the root manifest, the configuration's and `--config`'s over them".
- **`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`** shows up only in the list of variables a sandboxed test keeps under `affected`.

## Falls back to cargo

Each fallback prints "blaze: bug: <reason>; building with cargo, which blaze is never to do".

- **Whole invocation:** `--build-plan`/`--unit-graph`, `--message-format`, `-Z`, `--exclude`, more than one `--target`, or a target that is neither ELF nor Mach-O. For `check`, only the first of these applies.
- **Single build:** when "a cargo configuration file, or something a build script reads has changed since cargo last built". The same happens if a manifest or `Cargo.lock` changed.
  - Also when rust-analyzer finds an error, or when the daemon refuses or fails.
- **First use of each command line:** "The first use of each is a cargo build".
- **After memory eviction:** "the next build of its workspace is cargo's while a worker loads it again".
- **Intel Macs:** "x86-64 macOS is not a target blaze knows, so builds for it are cargo's."

**Note:** the doc contradicts itself here. The build section says nothing is handed to cargo, and that unsupported cases fail instead.

## Unsupported or failing cases

- **`build`/`run` fail on** "the targets `--bins`, `--examples`, `--tests`, `--benches` and `--all-targets` pick, several `--target`s, `--target-dir`,". The same goes for "`--message-format`, `-Z`, and `--build-plan` and `--unit-graph`".
- **Library types:** blaze can't write "a library whose crate types include `staticlib` or `dylib` when the build would write it" (#262).
- **Tests:** "A unit test with `harness = false`, several `--test`s and the other target flags fail the build and say so."
- **Code blaze can't compile** fails the build, for example "unsupported: f16 and f128".
- **Toolchain settings are ignored:** "It ignores `rust-toolchain`/`rust-toolchain.toml`, `rustup override`, `+toolchain`, `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`". It also ignores rustup's default and `RUSTC`.
- **Per-package optimization:** "a `[profile.release.package.<name>]` `opt-level` changes nothing". With `s` or `z`, the output is no smaller than `-O2`.
- **Windows:** "Windows has no sandbox yet, so there a build with build scripts or proc macros needs `BLAZE_SANDBOX=off`."
- **Doctests:** the daemon doesn't run them, and unlisted harness flags make them fail.

## Not covered in this excerpt

The text is truncated, and this part doesn't mention:

- `--no-default-features`
- `--locked`
- `[patch.crates-io]` path patches
- clang/mold linker settings in `.cargo/config.toml`
- `RUSTFLAGS` itself

The only linker details given are `rust-lld` on Windows and weak-definition linking on macOS.

content.content:
tmp=$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || mktemp -d -t blaze)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT TERM

if [ -n "$ARCHIVE" ]; then
    [ -f "$ARCHIVE" ] || fail "there is no file $ARCHIVE to install blaze from." "BLAZE_ARCHIVE names a release's archive, such as blaze-v0.2.0-$target.tar.gz."
    asset=$(basename "$ARCHIVE")
    tag=""
    say "Installing blaze from $asset for $machine..."
    cp "$ARCHIVE" "$tmp/$asset"
else
    releases="https://github.com/$REPO/releases"

    # The release: the one asked for; else canary's, the newest dated release, prerelease or
    # not; else stable's, GitHub's latest, which is never a prerelease, or the nightly build
    # before the first. The release feed needs no API token and has no rate limit, but lists
    # tags too, which have no release until release.yaml has built it: canary's is the newest
    # whose checksums are there.
    if [ -n "$VERSION" ]; then
        tag="v${VERSION#v}"
        [ "$VERSION" = nightly ] && tag=nightly
    elif [ "$CHANNEL" = canary ]; then
        fetch "$releases.atom" "$tmp/releases.atom" 2>"$tmp/error" ||
            fail "the list of blaze's releases could not be read; is the network up?" \
                "$(cat "$tmp/error")
$releases.atom"
        grep -o 'releases/tag/v[0-9][0-9]*\.[0-9][0-9]*\.[0-9][0-9]*"' "$tmp/releases.atom" |
            sed 's/^releases\/tag\/v//; s/"$//' | sort -t . -k 1,1nr -k 2,2nr -k 3,3nr > "$tmp/candidates" || true
        tag=""
        while read -r candidate; do
            if fetch "$releases/download/v$candidate/SHA256SUMS" "$tmp/SHA256SUMS" 2>/dev/null; then
                tag="v$candidate"
                break
            fi
            step "v$candidate has no release yet"
        done < "$tmp/candidates"
        [ -n "$tag" ] || fail "blaze has no canary release yet." "Releases: $releases"
    else
        latest=$(landing "$releases/latest" 2>/dev/null || true)
        case "$latest" in
            */releases/tag/*) tag="${latest##*/releases/tag/}" ;;
            *) tag=nightly ;;
        esac
    fi
    step "release $tag of $REPO ($CHANNEL)"

    if ! fetch "$releases/download/$tag/SHA256SUMS" "$tmp/SHA256SUMS" 2>"$tmp/error"; then
        if [ -n "$VERSION" ]; then
            fail "there is no blaze release $VERSION." "Releases: $releases"
        fi
        fail "the list of blaze's releases could not be read; is the network up?" \
            "$(cat "$tmp/error")
$releases/download/$tag/SHA256SUMS"
    fi

    asset="blaze-$tag-$target.tar.gz"
    awk -v n="$asset" '$2 == n || $2 == "*" n { found = 1 } END { exit !found }' "$tmp/SHA256SUMS" ||
        fail "blaze release $tag has no build for $machine." "Its files: $releases/tag/$tag"
    want=$(awk -v n="$asset" '$2 == n || $2 == "*" n { print $1; exit }' "$tmp/SHA256SUMS")

    if [ "$tag" = nightly ]; then shown="the nightly build"; else shown="blaze ${tag#v}"; fi
    if [ -z "$VERSION" ] && [ "$CHANNEL" = canary ]; then shown="$shown (canary)"; fi
    say "Installing $shown for $machine..."
    step "downloading $asset"
    fetch "$releases/download/$tag/$asset" "$tmp/$asset" 2>"$tmp/error" ||
        fail "the download of blaze stopped before it finished; running this again retries it." \
            "$(cat "$tmp/error")
$releases/download/$tag/$asset"
    got=$(sha256 "$tmp/$asset")
    [ "$got" = "$want" ] ||
        fail "the download is not the file the release published, so it was not installed. Running this again downloads it again." \
            "$asset: sha256 $got, the release's SHA256SUMS says $want"
fi

mkdir "$tmp/unpacked"
# -o: as root, tar gives files the archive's owner, which a container's user namespace may not have.
tar -xzof "$tmp/$asset" -C "$tmp/unpacked" 2>"$tmp/error" ||
    fail "the downloaded archive could not be unpacked." "$(cat "$tmp/error")"
unpacked="$tmp/unpacked/${asset%.tar.gz}"
# A release from before the rename (#270) has its programs' old names, by which they find each
# other: they keep them, but for the launchers of `blaze`, which is gone.
old_release=""
if [ ! -e "$unpacked/blaze-engine" ] && [ -x "$unpacked/ra-jit" ]; then # rename: old name
    old_release=1
    rm -f "$unpacked/cargo-blaze" "$unpacked/cargo-ra-jit" # rename: old name
fi

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Installing

Recipe that worked on 2026-10-17 for verifying editor UI changes without the Convex backend:

- **Port:** 5173 may belong to another project (interleave-app). Start twyne with `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 bun run dev.frontend`.
- **Headless Playwright:** importing `node_modules/playwright/index.mjs` from a scratch script works, but Chromium fails to launch (GLIBC error from a nix alsa-lib) unless run as `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node script.mjs`.

Instead, seed like `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()`: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, visit a routed blank page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")` in page context, then call saveFoliosToIdb / saveFolioContentToIdb / saveActiveFolioIdToIdb (+ `signin-toast-dismissed` meta, `twyne:editor:view:v1` with zenMode false).
- **T3 preview tool:** its viewport can be zoomed or scaled (innerWidth ≠ the requested size), and evaluate/snapshot time out on heavy pages. Prefer the headless script for measurements.

- **Running e2e:** with the dev server on 5174, `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 npx playwright test <file>` works.
  - Screenshot suites (instruments, instrument-dock, instrument-room, living-desk) must run under `--config playwright.visual.config.ts`. It starts its own server on 5187 and compares against the committed `e2e/visual-baselines/`. The default config writes stray `e2e/*-snapshots/` folders; delete them afterwards.
  - About 38 default-config e2e tests already failed at HEAD bfa07af1 (checked on 2026-10-17 against a clean worktree). The causes:
    - The Pagination extension was unregistered in 0cb77885, so `__twynePagination` never appears. This breaks all of pagination and formatting, and most of drag-selection.
    - The "Go to page" combobox needs the Typst proof, which never typesets here. This breaks editor-declutter.
    - Tests expect a visible `.twyne-toolbar`, Bold, or read-aloud control, but zen is now the default and those sit in the collapsed Compositor. This breaks __responsive, select-all and read-aloud.
    - Tests expect a "File ▾" button and other masthead and drawer flows that have since changed. This breaks import and dossier-persistence.
  - Before blaming a change, run the same files against `git worktree add --detach /tmp/twyne-base HEAD` on port 5175 and diff the failing test names. The BYOK and drop-caret tests flake.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Render Twyne in an isolated Xvfb display; never use the user's desktop."""
from pathlib import Path

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--binary", required=True)
parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
parser.add_argument("--geometry", help="Write observed interface bounds from the UI-test build")
parser.add_argument("--width", type=int, default=1280)
parser.add_argument("--height", type=int, default=860)
parser.add_argument("--state", choices=["quiet", "writing", "slash", "slash-filtered", "slash-form", "slash-endnote", "slash-footnote", "slash-mermaid", "slash-math-inline", "slash-math-block", "desk", "drawer", "board", "source", "proof", "split", "dossier", "settings", "account", "account-error", "versions", "house", "library", "flow", "tools", "marginalia", "margin-thread", "margin-composer", "cast", "editors", "analysis", "rubric", "galley", "apparatus", "apparatus-page", "sentence-lab", "rhythm-strip", "claim-check", "reader-questions"], default="quiet")
parser.add_argument("--fixture")
parser.add_argument("--comments")
parser.add_argument("--comments-folio")
parser.add_argument("--cast")
parser.add_argument("--cast-folio")
parser.add_argument("--rubric")
parser.add_argument("--rubric-folio")
parser.add_argument("--apparatus")
parser.add_argument("--apparatus-folio")
args = parser.parse_args()
if not 320 <= args.width <= 3840 or not 360 <= args.height <= 2160:
    parser.error("Capture size must be 320–3840 by 360–2160 pixels.")
if bool(args.comments) != bool(args.comments_folio):
    parser.error("--comments and --comments-folio must be provided together")
if bool(args.cast) != bool(args.cast_folio):
    parser.error("--cast and --cast-folio must be provided together")
if bool(args.rubric) != bool(args.rubric_folio):
    parser.error("--rubric and --rubric-folio must be provided together")
if bool(args.apparatus) != bool(args.apparatus_folio):
    parser.error("--apparatus and --apparatus-folio must be provided together")
for executable in ("Xvfb", "xwd", "magick"):
    if not shutil.which(executable):
        parser.error(f"{executable} is required; run inside the project's Devenv shell.")

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="twyne-native-render-") as temporary:
    root = Path(temporary)
    # Let Xvfb allocate an unused display, with no TCP listener.
    read_fd, write_fd = os.pipe()
    # GPUI's X11 backend offsets a new window by two pixels. Leave room for
    # the full client and capture that window, so root-screen position never
    # shifts the comparison or clips the application's right edge.
    screen = f"{args.width + 4}x{args.height + 4}x24"
    server = subprocess.Popen(["Xvfb", "-displayfd", str(write_fd), "-screen", "0", screen, "-nolisten", "tcp"], pass_fds=(write_fd,), stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    os.close(write_fd)
    app = None
    try:
        with os.fdopen(read_fd) as display_file:
            number = display_file.readline().strip()
        if not number:
            raise RuntimeError("The isolated display did not start.")
        environment = os.environ.copy()
        environment.pop("WAYLAND_DISPLAY", None)

My E2B key checks out with no existing templates or sandboxes, and the default "base" template is publicly available but its resources (around 2 vCPU/512MB) seem too limited for building gpui, which needs more RAM. I'm now considering whether a custom template with higher resources would be needed instead.

Setting up a remote build farm (custom template with Rust, Xvfb, lavapipe, ImageMagick, bun, Chromium, code sync, artifact retrieval) is its own project with real upfront cost, so it's probably better to delegate that setup to a parallel Terra lane while read-only inventory lanes proceed without builds, and run the harness lane locally in the meantime. Round 2 fix lanes can then use remote builders once ready, falling back to limited local concurrency otherwise. I want to verify E2B's plan limits before committing to this approach.

For the swarm, I'm planning Lane H as the local parity harness that handles builds directly, and Lane R as a remote build/capture runner using E2B as primary with Railway/Cloudflare as fallback — syncing a worktree to a sandbox built from a template that replicates the devenv toolchain (ideally with Nix so `devenv shell` works identically), running cargo/test/clippy/capture commands, streaming logs, and pulling artifacts back, with some mechanism to persist the cargo target cache between runs.

Then Lanes G1–G5 are read-only completeness inventories that commit markdown/JSON fixtures per group without touching cargo. I'm considering whether these inventory lanes should also capture web reference states beyond the standard 40, including error/empty/menu/dialog states, and listing gaps as "capture states to add" — settling on 7 total concurrent lanes since the user wants maximum parallelism, though I need to account for project setup steps like bun install even in the read-only lanes.

I'm deciding inventory lanes still need worktree isolation despite being read-only, each writing to a distinct file path, and planning to fast-forward merge feat/native-port-ai-audio into the working branch. Now I'm defining Lane H in detail: after merging, it builds `capture-web.ts`, a Playwright-based tool that spins up a dev server on a free port, seeds IndexedDB following the same pattern as the existing e2e seed helper, and captures reference screenshots from the web app.

Continuing Lane H's design, I'm sketching out `capture-native-all.py` to loop through native UI states with the same fixture and save native screenshots, plus a `compare.py` script that uses ImageMagick to diff web vs native screenshots per state (both pixel AE and perceptual RMSE), generating a sortable HTML report with diff images alongside JSON output, all driven from a shared fixture document used across both native and browser renderers.
