input.title: Parity harness: web + native capture and pixel diff report
input.task:
Build the pixel-parity harness for the Twyne native desktop port. Twyne is a web app (Qwik + Convex) referred to as "Source"; `desktop/gpui` is its GPUI/Rust port, which must match Source pixel for pixel at 1280×860. Before anything else, run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio` in your worktree. That branch has the newest native work. Then read `desktop/gpui/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `desktop/gpui/PORT_PLAN.md` ("Verification") and `desktop/gpui/fixtures/chrome/README.md`.

## What exists
- `desktop/gpui/tools/capture-native.py` renders the native app in an isolated Xvfb display. It takes `--binary`, `--state <name>` (about 40 named states: quiet, writing, slash*, desk, drawer, board, source, proof, split, dossier, settings, account, account-error, versions, house, library, flow, tools, marginalia, margin-thread, margin-composer, cast, editors, analysis, rubric, galley, apparatus, apparatus-page, sentence-lab, rhythm-strip, claim-check, reader-questions), `--fixture`, plus `--comments/--cast/--rubric/--apparatus` fixture pairs. The states are applied in `desktop/gpui/src/app.rs::set_capture_state`. It needs a `ui-tests` build: `devenv shell -- cargo build --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml --bin twyne-desktop`. Build the document helper first with `devenv shell -- bun run desktop.gpui.build-helper`.
- The browser side has only scattered per-feature reference scripts, for example `fixtures/settings/generate-web-reference.ts`, `fixtures/house/generate.ts`, `fixtures/editor/capture-flow-web.ts` and `fixtures/connected-work/capture-account-source.ts`. Reuse their seeding and driving patterns.
- Web recipe that works on this machine:
  - Run the dev server on a free port: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=<port> bun run dev.frontend`. 5173 may belong to another project.
  - Run Playwright via `node_modules/playwright`, under `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH`; Nix's alsa-lib otherwise breaks Chromium.
  - Seed IndexedDB the way `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()` does: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, open a blank routed page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")`, then save folios, content and the active folio id. Also set the `signin-toast-dismissed` meta and `twyne:editor:view:v1`.

## Build
Put the code in `desktop/gpui/tools/parity/` and write outputs to `desktop/gpui/target/parity/` (not committed):
1. `capture-web.ts`. For every native state name, drive Source into the equivalent UI and screenshot `web/<state>.png`.
   - Use the same documents and panel data the native capture uses. Prefer one shared fixture set, for example `desktop/gpui/fixtures/marginalia/browser-manuscript.html` plus the existing comments/cast/rubric/apparatus fixtures. Seed the web equivalents.
   - Viewport 1280×860 at DPR 1, reduced motion, a frozen clock (`page.clock`), `document.fonts.ready`, and settled animations.
   - The theme and every preference must match native defaults.
2. `capture-native-all.py`. Capture every state with the same fixtures into `native/<state>.png`.
3. `compare.py`. For each state:
   - compute a pixel diff with ImageMagick (`compare -metric AE -fuzz 2%`), reporting the % of differing pixels, plus RMSE;
   - write `diff/<state>.png` and a `side/<state>.png` side-by-side;
   - write `report.json` and `report.html`, sorted worst first, showing web | native | diff per state.
4. `run.ts`, exposed as package.json script `desktop.gpui.parity` with `--states a,b` filtering. It starts the dev server, captures both sides, compares, and prints the summary table.

## Rules
- Tooling only. Do NOT change app code in `src/` or `desktop/gpui/src/`.
- If a state can't be reproduced on one side, record it in `report.json` with the exact reason, and keep going. That includes a native capture state that crashes or a web surface you can't reach. Those reasons are findings.
- If the native and web documents can't be made identical for a state, say so explicitly rather than comparing different content.
- Keep everything isolated: never use the user's display, and use temp data dirs.

## Finish
Run the full pass once. Commit the tooling, but not the PNGs, on your worktree branch with a plain-English message, and do not push. Your final report must cover:
- the summary table (state → % differing pixels, RMSE);
- states not reproducible on either side, with reasons;
- the absolute path to `report.html`;
- the exact commands to rerun.

input.title: Remote build runner on E2B for the native port
input.task:
Build a remote build-and-capture runner so that many parallel agents can compile and test the Twyne native desktop app (`desktop/gpui`, GPUI/Rust) off this machine. Locally, each worktree's `ui-tests` build needs about 12 GB of disk; free space is about 55 GB and RAM is 31 GB. Before anything else, run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio` in your worktree.

## Accounts available
Never print, log or commit secrets.
- **E2B (preferred):** the API key is from `skate get e2b_api_key@secrets`, and the account currently has no templates or sandboxes. Use the official `e2b` JS SDK (add it as a devDependency) or the REST API.
- **Railway:** the `railway` CLI is logged in, as a fallback.
- **Cloudflare:** the token is from `skate get cloudflare@secrets`, and the account id from `skate get cloudflare_account_id@default`. This is a fallback for Cloudflare Sandbox/Containers.
Pick E2B unless it truly can't do this, and explain the choice.

## Build
Put the code in `desktop/gpui/tools/remote/`.
1. **A sandbox template that reproduces the project toolchain faithfully.** Best is Nix plus devenv inside the template, so that `devenv shell -- <cmd>` behaves exactly as it does locally; the repo's `devenv.nix`/`devenv.lock` pin Rust 1.98.1, the clang linker, Xvfb, Mesa lavapipe, ImageMagick, alsa-lib and pipewire. If that's impractical, use an equivalent: rustup 1.98.1 plus apt packages. Either way, prove that the toolchain matches.
   - Include bun, plus the Playwright Chromium dependencies for web captures.
   - Choose CPU, RAM and disk generous enough for the gpui/typst build (≥8 vCPU and ≥16 GB RAM if the plan allows). Report the limits you actually got.
   - Build the template remotely; there is no local Docker requirement.
2. **`run.ts <worktree> -- <command...>`.**
   - Sync the worktree's tracked and modified files to a sandbox. Use `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard`; exclude `target/` and `node_modules/`.
   - Run the command in the toolchain environment, streaming output with the exit code preserved.
   - Pull back requested artifacts with `--pull <glob>`, for example `desktop/gpui/target/parity/**` or test logs.
   - Keep a warm Cargo target dir and registry between runs for the same lane, using `--lane <name>` with E2B pause/resume or a persistent volume. Without that, every run cold-builds.
   - Also support `--keep`, a `stop <lane>` command, and a `list` of live sandboxes.
3. **Prove it end to end.** Using the integration branch, remotely run:
   - `devenv shell -- cargo test --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml settings`;
   - one native capture: build the `ui-tests` binary and the doc helper (`bun run desktop.gpui.build-helper`), then `python3 desktop/gpui/tools/capture-native.py --binary desktop/gpui/target/debug/twyne-desktop --state quiet --output /tmp/q.png`, pulling the PNG back.
   Report cold and warm timings.
4. **Document it** in `desktop/gpui/tools/remote/README.md`, written so another agent can use it from one paragraph. Add a package.json script `desktop.gpui.remote`.

## Rules
- Shut down every sandbox you start; leave nothing running unless it's a paused lane cache, and list those.
- Report the spend or quota you used.
- Don't change app code.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch with a plain-English message; do not push. Your final report must cover the chosen platform and why, the template id, the resource limits, the cold and warm timings, the exact usage, and anything that didn't work.

input.title: Parity harness: web + native capture and pixel diff report
input.task:
Build the pixel-parity harness for the Twyne native desktop port. Twyne is a web app (Qwik + Convex) referred to as "Source"; `desktop/gpui` is its GPUI/Rust port, which must match Source pixel for pixel at 1280×860. Before anything else, run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio` in your worktree. That branch has the newest native work. Then read `desktop/gpui/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `desktop/gpui/PORT_PLAN.md` ("Verification") and `desktop/gpui/fixtures/chrome/README.md`.

## What exists
- `desktop/gpui/tools/capture-native.py` renders the native app in an isolated Xvfb display. It takes `--binary`, `--state <name>` (about 40 named states: quiet, writing, slash*, desk, drawer, board, source, proof, split, dossier, settings, account, account-error, versions, house, library, flow, tools, marginalia, margin-thread, margin-composer, cast, editors, analysis, rubric, galley, apparatus, apparatus-page, sentence-lab, rhythm-strip, claim-check, reader-questions), `--fixture`, plus `--comments/--cast/--rubric/--apparatus` fixture pairs. The states are applied in `desktop/gpui/src/app.rs::set_capture_state`. It needs a `ui-tests` build: `devenv shell -- cargo build --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml --bin twyne-desktop`. Build the document helper first with `devenv shell -- bun run desktop.gpui.build-helper`.
- The browser side has only scattered per-feature reference scripts, for example `fixtures/settings/generate-web-reference.ts`, `fixtures/house/generate.ts`, `fixtures/editor/capture-flow-web.ts` and `fixtures/connected-work/capture-account-source.ts`. Reuse their seeding and driving patterns.
- Web recipe that works on this machine:
  - Run the dev server on a free port: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=<port> bun run dev.frontend`. 5173 may belong to another project.
  - Run Playwright via `node_modules/playwright`, under `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH`; Nix's alsa-lib otherwise breaks Chromium.
  - Seed IndexedDB the way `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()` does: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, open a blank routed page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")`, then save folios, content and the active folio id. Also set the `signin-toast-dismissed` meta and `twyne:editor:view:v1`.

## Build
Put the code in `desktop/gpui/tools/parity/` and write outputs to `desktop/gpui/target/parity/` (not committed):
1. `capture-web.ts`. For every native state name, drive Source into the equivalent UI and screenshot `web/<state>.png`.
   - Use the same documents and panel data the native capture uses. Prefer one shared fixture set, for example `desktop/gpui/fixtures/marginalia/browser-manuscript.html` plus the existing comments/cast/rubric/apparatus fixtures. Seed the web equivalents.
   - Viewport 1280×860 at DPR 1, reduced motion, a frozen clock (`page.clock`), `document.fonts.ready`, and settled animations.
   - The theme and every preference must match native defaults.
2. `capture-native-all.py`. Capture every state with the same fixtures into `native/<state>.png`.
3. `compare.py`. For each state:
   - compute a pixel diff with ImageMagick (`compare -metric AE -fuzz 2%`), reporting the % of differing pixels, plus RMSE;
   - write `diff/<state>.png` and a `side/<state>.png` side-by-side;
   - write `report.json` and `report.html`, sorted worst first, showing web | native | diff per state.
4. `run.ts`, exposed as package.json script `desktop.gpui.parity` with `--states a,b` filtering. It starts the dev server, captures both sides, compares, and prints the summary table.

## Rules
- Tooling only. Do NOT change app code in `src/` or `desktop/gpui/src/`.
- If a state can't be reproduced on one side, record it in `report.json` with the exact reason, and keep going. That includes a native capture state that crashes or a web surface you can't reach. Those reasons are findings.
- If the native and web documents can't be made identical for a state, say so explicitly rather than comparing different content.
- Keep everything isolated: never use the user's display, and use temp data dirs.

## Finish
Run the full pass once. Commit the tooling, but not the PNGs, on your worktree branch with a plain-English message, and do not push. Your final report must cover:
- the summary table (state → % differing pixels, RMSE);
- states not reproducible on either side, with reasons;
- the absolute path to `report.html`;
- the exact commands to rerun.

input.title: Remote build runner on E2B for the native port
input.task:
Build a remote build-and-capture runner so that many parallel agents can compile and test the Twyne native desktop app (`desktop/gpui`, GPUI/Rust) off this machine. Locally, each worktree's `ui-tests` build needs about 12 GB of disk; free space is about 55 GB and RAM is 31 GB. Before anything else, run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio` in your worktree.

## Accounts available
Never print, log or commit secrets.
- **E2B (preferred):** the API key is from `skate get e2b_api_key@secrets`, and the account currently has no templates or sandboxes. Use the official `e2b` JS SDK (add it as a devDependency) or the REST API.
- **Railway:** the `railway` CLI is logged in, as a fallback.
- **Cloudflare:** the token is from `skate get cloudflare@secrets`, and the account id from `skate get cloudflare_account_id@default`. This is a fallback for Cloudflare Sandbox/Containers.
Pick E2B unless it truly can't do this, and explain the choice.

## Build
Put the code in `desktop/gpui/tools/remote/`.
1. **A sandbox template that reproduces the project toolchain faithfully.** Best is Nix plus devenv inside the template, so that `devenv shell -- <cmd>` behaves exactly as it does locally; the repo's `devenv.nix`/`devenv.lock` pin Rust 1.98.1, the clang linker, Xvfb, Mesa lavapipe, ImageMagick, alsa-lib and pipewire. If that's impractical, use an equivalent: rustup 1.98.1 plus apt packages. Either way, prove that the toolchain matches.
   - Include bun, plus the Playwright Chromium dependencies for web captures.
   - Choose CPU, RAM and disk generous enough for the gpui/typst build (≥8 vCPU and ≥16 GB RAM if the plan allows). Report the limits you actually got.
   - Build the template remotely; there is no local Docker requirement.
2. **`run.ts <worktree> -- <command...>`.**
   - Sync the worktree's tracked and modified files to a sandbox. Use `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard`; exclude `target/` and `node_modules/`.
   - Run the command in the toolchain environment, streaming output with the exit code preserved.
   - Pull back requested artifacts with `--pull <glob>`, for example `desktop/gpui/target/parity/**` or test logs.
   - Keep a warm Cargo target dir and registry between runs for the same lane, using `--lane <name>` with E2B pause/resume or a persistent volume. Without that, every run cold-builds.
   - Also support `--keep`, a `stop <lane>` command, and a `list` of live sandboxes.
3. **Prove it end to end.** Using the integration branch, remotely run:
   - `devenv shell -- cargo test --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml settings`;
   - one native capture: build the `ui-tests` binary and the doc helper (`bun run desktop.gpui.build-helper`), then `python3 desktop/gpui/tools/capture-native.py --binary desktop/gpui/target/debug/twyne-desktop --state quiet --output /tmp/q.png`, pulling the PNG back.
   Report cold and warm timings.
4. **Document it** in `desktop/gpui/tools/remote/README.md`, written so another agent can use it from one paragraph. Add a package.json script `desktop.gpui.remote`.

## Rules
- Shut down every sandbox you start; leave nothing running unless it's a paused lane cache, and list those.
- Report the spend or quota you used.
- Don't change app code.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch with a plain-English message; do not push. Your final report must cover the chosen platform and why, the template id, the resource limits, the cold and warm timings, the exact usage, and anything that didn't work.

Builds stay cached between runs, and Railway or Cloudflare is the fallback. That way fix lanes don't each need 12 GB here. |

Produce an exhaustive completeness inventory of the native desktop port against the web app, for one surface group. Twyne's web app ("Source": Qwik, in `src/`) is being ported to a GPUI/Rust app in `desktop/gpui/src`, which must match Source in pixels and UX at 1280×860. The reference desktop experience is `desktop/main.ts`.

First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`. Read `desktop/gpui/ARCHITECTURE.md` (especially the insert-menu rules) and `PORT_PLAN.md`, but verify everything in code; PORT_PLAN's claims are not evidence.

**Your scope: the slash/insert menu and every insert form.**
- the catalog, search/filtering, keyboard navigation, grouping and icons;
- every insert command and its form, parameters, validation, preview and cancel/commit behaviour: table, footnote, endnote, math inline/block, mermaid, images (all import paths), citations, links, and every other catalog entry;

input.title: Parity inventory: Rubric and Galley
input.task:
Exhaustive parity inventory for one narrow scope. Twyne's web app ("Source": Qwik, in `src/`) is being ported to GPUI/Rust in `desktop/gpui/src`. Native must match Source in pixels and UX at 1280×860; the reference is `desktop/main.ts`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then skim `desktop/gpui/ARCHITECTURE.md`. Claims in `PORT_PLAN.md` are not evidence; verify everything in code.

**Scope:** Rubric and Galley. That means every Source rubric/galley component and its supporting utils and background services, against native `rubric*.rs` and `rubric_view*.rs`.

**Method** (you'll be judged on coverage):
1. List every Source file in scope at the top of `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/rubric.md`, with a "covered" column.
2. Walk each file's JSX and handlers. Each of these is one item: every element with an event handler, every form control and every `role`/`aria-*`, every conditional render branch (each one is a state), every user-visible string, every handled key, every animation or transition class, and every persisted key.
3. Find the native counterpart and classify the item as Matches, Partial (state the exact difference), Missing, or Native-only, citing `file:line` on both sides.
4. Write `rubric.json`: an array of `{id, surface, item, kind, source_ref, native_ref, status, gap, capture_state_needed, effort}`.
   - `capture_state_needed` is an existing `--state` from `desktop/gpui/tools/capture-native.py`, a proposed new state, or `"behavioral"`.
   - `effort` is S, M or L.
5. Commit after each file with `devenv shell -- git commit -m "..."`. The hook needs `prek`, which only exists inside devenv.

Don't modify app code and don't push. Don't finish until every file in scope is covered.

**Final report:** files covered N/N, item counts by status, the top 15 gaps by user visibility, and proposed capture states.

content.text:
The swarm is now 23 Terra lanes running in parallel.

The first audit round came back far too thin: board had 6 items, dossier 3, writing surface 10, connected 25. Terra lanes kept stopping after a small slice. So I split every group into narrow lanes, one per surface, with a method that can be checked. Each lane lists every Source file in its scope, then walks each file's markup and handlers. Every control, conditional branch (each one is a state), visible string, handled key, animation and persisted key becomes an item, classified against native with `file:line` on both sides. Lanes commit after each file, so an interruption loses nothing, and report coverage as files covered N/N.

**Running now:**
- **Tools:** the parity harness (browser vs native pixel diff for every capture state, with an HTML report) and the E2B remote build runner.
- **Chrome, settings and navigation:** 1 lane.
- **Writing surface:** 4 lanes, for find/compositor/formatting, insert forms, Typst views/pagination/Zen, and input/history/clipboard/extensions.
- **Editorial board:** 7 lanes, for board shell/Cast, Rubric/Galley, Marginalia, Apparatus, Tools/Versions, In-flow, and the instruments.
- **Projects and documents:** 4 lanes, for Dossier, onboarding/starters, import/export/data, and the other reachable routes.
- **Connected features:** 5 lanes, for AI providers/request states, sign-in, sync/sharing/publishing, wallet/data controls, and voice/Live.

The connected-feature lanes also name each network connection native still lacks, so the fix round can tell real gaps apart from missing backend wiring.

When the inventories and the pixel report are in, I'll merge them into one ranked gap list and start the fix lanes on the remote runner.

A better approach is to make the enumeration itself mechanical rather than relying on model diligence: I'll build a script that parses the TSX source files and automatically extracts event handlers, conditional branches, string literals, aria attributes, and keys into a candidate item list with source references. Then each lane's job becomes simple classification against native equivalents, making "continue" just mean processing the next batch — turning coverage into something measurable and chunkable instead of something the models might skip.

Writing the TypeScript enumeration script...

Given the likely scale — thousands of items — I'm thinking about how to keep lane turns bounded: assign each lane just 1-2 files per task so one turn suffices, and fan out many parallel lanes rather than having one lane churn through everything, since turn length seems to be the real constraint on throughput.

But creating a fresh isolated worktree per task is way too expensive at that scale — 150 worktrees would blow past disk limits — so I should reuse a persistent thread per lane and feed it a queue of files sequentially, having it report back what remains after each turn so I can dispatch the next chunk without over-concurrency.

Alternatively lanes could skip worktrees entirely and just write outputs to a shared scratch directory while reading source directly from the integration worktree path, though that risks lanes clobbering a shared dirty checkout if I'm not careful instructing them to only read, not write, there.

My plan is to quickly write the enumerator myself, run it against the integration worktree to produce per-file item skeletons, check the counts, then hand off file queues to the ~24 existing lane threads by scope, telling each to classify its pre-enumerated items, add any the enumerator missed, and commit per file as they finish. The harness lane can keep running independently in the background. I should check the tools-versions task status first, then get the enumerator written, while keeping the user's actual goal in mind — making sure every surface of the desktop app is covered.

I confirm TypeScript is available since node_modules/typescript exists in the main checkout and the integration worktree now has node_modules from bun install, so I can run a TS script via bun. I'm now scoping the enumerator to pull items from TSX/TS files in src/components and src/routes (plus select utils), extracting things like JSX event handler attributes as "interaction" items labeled by element tag and attribute.

Form elements like input, textarea, select, and button get merged into "control" items with their handlers listed, and role/aria attributes get folded into those same element entries. I'm also flagging conditional rendering patterns involving JSX operands as "state" items, capturing user-visible strings (JSXText plus attributes like title, placeholder, aria-label, alt, label) as "copy" items, detecting key-based logic like `.key === "X"` or `e.key` switches as "key" items, and tracking localStorage calls for persistence-related items.

Persistence calls (setItem, sessionStorage, idb helpers) map to "persist" items, and Tailwind classes with "animate-" or "transition" map to "motion" items. I'm deciding on element-level granularity—one item per JSX element with handlers/roles/aria, separate copy items per text block—acknowledging this could generate thousands of entries but planning to just run it and observe. For output, I'll place the enumeration tool at `desktop/gpui/tools/parity-enumerate/enumerate.ts` to avoid conflicting with the harness lane's tools directory, then start writing it.

But creating a fresh isolated worktree per task is way too expensive at that scale — 150 worktrees would blow past disk limits — so I should reuse a persistent thread per lane and feed it a queue of files sequentially, having it report back what remains after each turn so I can dispatch the next chunk without over-concurrency.

Alternatively lanes could skip worktrees entirely and just write outputs to a shared scratch directory while reading source directly from the integration worktree path, though that risks lanes clobbering a shared dirty checkout if I'm not careful instructing them to only read, not write, there.

My plan is to quickly write the enumerator myself, run it against the integration worktree to produce per-file item skeletons, check the counts, then hand off file queues to the ~24 existing lane threads by scope, telling each to classify its pre-enumerated items, add any the enumerator missed, and commit per file as they finish. The harness lane can keep running independently in the background. I should check the tools-versions task status first, then get the enumerator written, while keeping the user's actual goal in mind — making sure every surface of the desktop app is covered.

I'm now scoping the enumerator to pull items from TSX/TS files in src/components and src/routes (plus select utils), extracting things like JSX event handler attributes as "interaction" items labeled by element tag and attribute.

Form elements like input, textarea, select, and button get merged into "control" items with their handlers listed, and role/aria attributes get folded into those same element entries. Persistence calls (setItem, sessionStorage, idb helpers) map to "persist" items, and Tailwind classes with "animate-" or "transition" map to "motion" items. I'm deciding on element-level granularity—one item per JSX element with handlers/roles/aria, separate copy items per text block—acknowledging this could generate thousands of entries but planning to just run it and observe. Now I'm thinking about scoping and chunking: based on throughput from earlier turns (roughly 40–110 items per lane), a 72k-line app might generate 15–25k items, which would require too many chunks to be practical. I'm weighing whether to dedupe trivial items or classify at a higher component level instead of item-level, but recognizing that true parity requires item-level detail, so I'm leaning toward a staged approach where the extractor first produces the full candidate list before prioritizing.

I'm settling on a plan: auto-match copy strings and aria-labels/titles against native Rust source via substring comparison (normalizing whitespace) to automatically flag "present" vs "missing" candidates, leaving only handlers and state logic for manual judgment. content.text:
The audit round has given me what I need, but not the way I planned it. Most inventory lanes stopped after 0–3 files, even with narrow scopes. They were honest about it, but per-item judgment across about 72k lines of Source is more than a Terra turn can carry.

So I built the checklist mechanically instead. `desktop/gpui/tools/parity-inventory/extract.ts` is committed on the integration branch as `a9a25d86`. It parses all 173 Source component and route files and lists 8,744 items: every handler, control, ARIA attribute, rendered state, piece of copy, handled key, persisted key and animation. It also checks whether each user-visible string exists anywhere in the native Rust.

**Overall, 36% of Source's copy exists natively.** By area:

| Mostly unported | Partly ported | Mostly there |
|---|---|---|
| instruments 9%, desk/usage 0–20%, Settings 13–19%, living desk 17%, Live voice 12%, speech player 16%, folio menu 24%, dialogs/toasts ~0% | in-flow 33%, writing tools 30%, personas 44%, onboarding 57%, House 58% | editor 61%, rubric 61%, revisions 74%, citations 76%, comments 80% |

**Next is the port round.** I'll run about 13 Terra port lanes, each owning one area's native modules and using that area's extracted items as its checklist. Each one adds capture states and proves the result with the parity harness against the browser. They'll build on E2B, since a local build takes about 12 GB and only 39 GB is free. So the port lanes start as soon as the remote-runner lane reports. The harness lane is also close to done.

**Public pages:** landing, pricing, docs, blog, FAQ, terms, privacy and downloads will open in the system browser rather than being rebuilt natively, unless you want those native too.

# Desktop parity harness

Captures each named state in Source (the web app, through Playwright) and in the
native app (isolated Xvfb), at 1280 × 860 and DPR 1. It then writes a pixel
diff and side-by-side images per state, with `report.html` worst first.

```sh
devenv shell -- bun run desktop.gpui.build-helper
devenv shell -- cargo build --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml --bin twyne-desktop
devenv shell -- bun run desktop.gpui.parity                      # every state
devenv shell -- bun run desktop.gpui.parity --states quiet,desk  # some states
```

Outputs go to `desktop/gpui/target/parity/`, and each run replaces them. RMSE
is normalised to 0–1. The differing-pixel percentage uses a 2% fuzz.

## Adding a state

1. **Native side.** Add the state to `--capture-state` in `src/main.rs`,
   `App::set_capture_state` in `src/app.rs`, and the `--state` choices in
   `tools/capture-native.py`.
2. **Source side.** Add `drivers/<state>.ts`. It default-exports a `Driver`
   (see `driver.ts`): view preferences, route, extra seeding, a readiness
   wait, and the interactions that reach the state. A state without a driver
   is reported as unmapped. It is never captured as a stand-in.
3. **Shared list.** Append the state name to `states.json`.
4. **Same content check.** Once Source and native show the same content and
   panel data for the state, set `verified: true`. Until then the pair is
   still scored, but the report marks it unverified.

Every state uses the shared manuscript
(`fixtures/marginalia/browser-manuscript.html`) and comments. The panel
fixtures `capture-native-all.py` passes to native (cast, rubric, apparatus)
need equivalent Source seeding in the driver's `seed`.
EOF

input.content:
# Port lanes: shared rules

Each port lane makes one area of the native desktop app
(`desktop/gpui/src`) match Source (the web app, `src/`) exactly at
1280 × 860. "Exactly" covers layout, spacing, type, colour, copy, states,
interactions, keyboard and persistence. Source wins wherever the two differ.
Native-only behaviour stays only where the platform needs it.

## Start

```sh
git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio
```

Read `desktop/gpui/ARCHITECTURE.md`, which covers module ownership, the
UTF-16 rules and the coordinator pattern, and `desktop/gpui/tools/parity/README.md`.

## Your checklist

1. **The complete list.** Run
   `bun desktop/gpui/tools/parity-inventory/extract.ts --out /tmp/parity-<lane>`,
   then filter `/tmp/parity-<lane>/items.jsonl` to the Source files in your
   scope. Every handler, control, ARIA attribute, rendered state, piece of
   copy, handled key, persisted key and motion class in those files must end
   up matched in native. `copyNative: true` only means the string exists
   somewhere in native, not that the surface matches.
2. **Earlier findings.** Use the `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/<area>.json`
   file your lane names, if it has one. It holds `file:line`-cited findings
   from the audit round. They are a head start, not the full list.

Keep `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/progress/<lane>.json` current. It is an
array of `{item_id, status: "done"|"blocked"|"not-applicable", native_ref, note}`
for every checklist item in scope. Commit it with your code.

## How to work

- Go surface by surface. Port the markup structure, styles (resolve Source's
  Tailwind/CSS to exact values), copy, states and interactions. Then add
  tests and capture states, then commit, then go on to the next surface.
- **Commit after every surface** with
  `devenv shell -- git commit -m "<plain English>"`. The pre-commit hook needs
  `prek`, which only exists inside devenv. Do not push.
- **Do not stop early.** Keep going until every item in scope is done,
  blocked (with the exact reason) or not applicable (with the reason). If you
  run low on room, commit and end with a precise list of what remains.
- **No fake success.** Do not ship a control that pretends to work. If a
  feature needs a backend transport that native does not have, build the
  transport if your lane owns it. Otherwise render Source's own
  unavailable/offline state and mark the item blocked, naming the transport.

## Files you may touch

- Your lane's feature modules and its own `src/app/<feature>_coordinator.rs`.
- **Shared host files**, kept as small as possible and in one block with a
  `// <lane>` comment: `src/app.rs`, `src/app/room_layout.rs`, `src/main.rs`,
  `src/lib.rs`, `tools/capture-native.py`, `tools/parity/states.json`, and
  theme or chrome. Never reformat or reorder code you do not own.
- New crates are allowed only if your lane truly needs one. Name it in the
  report, because `Cargo.lock` conflicts land on the coordinator.

## Proving it

- **Capture states.** For each surface and important state in your scope, add
  a native capture state in `src/main.rs`, `App::set_capture_state` and
  `tools/capture-native.py`. Add the matching Source driver in
  `tools/parity/drivers/<state>.ts`, and append the state to

- Data controls: native export (range-scoped), consent and the local deletion flows.

**Native modules you own:** new `desk/` modules and `living_desk` modules.

**Capture states:** `desk-summary`, `desk-activity`, `desk-usage-signed-out`, `desk-forecast`, `living-desk`, `data-controls`, `data-controls-delete-confirm`.

input.title: Port: Live voice desk with local and hosted transports
input.task:
Lane `live-voice`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then read and follow `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`. It is the contract for this work: checklist, commits, proving, remote builds and report.

- `src/components/ui/live-voice-desk*`.

- The relay protocol in `scripts/live-voice-relay.mjs`.

**Earlier findings:** `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/voice.json`. The native Talk control is disabled, and there is no mounted desk, credentials, consent, websocket or receipt settlement.

**What to build:**
1. **The native desk UI, exactly as Source.** The `find-compositor` lane makes the compositor's Talk control dispatch an event; handle it.
2. **The hosted transport.** Make a native websocket connection to the Not Organic gateway `/v1/live/sessions` with the same DPoP/idempotency/budget handshake the relay builds. Credentials come from the account session, which the `account` lane owns. Build against an interface, and render Source's sign-in-required state when there is no session.
3. **A local transport.** Use a local realtime speech model on loopback, with LFM3-Audio from Liquid AI as the target. Investigate what local server and protocol it exposes, and adapt to Source's event contract. If a usable local runtime isn't available yet, say exactly what is missing.
4. **Audio.** Use `native_audio::live_voice` plus the CPAL device backend for mic and playback.

Add a tungstenite-style websocket crate if needed, and name it.

**Native modules you own:** `native_audio/live_voice.rs` and new `live_voice/` modules.

**Capture states:** `live-voice-desk`, `live-voice-connecting`, `live-voice-listening`, `live-voice-proposal`, `live-voice-error`, `live-voice-signed-out`. Prove the protocol with a hermetic fake gateway test.

input.task:
Lane `account`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then read and follow `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`. It is the contract for this work: checklist, commits, proving, remote builds and report. Also read `docs/notorganic-native-identity.md`.

**Scope (Source).**
- `src/components/auth/**`: the account menu's signed-in parts, sign-in, avatar and initials, sign-out, and the sign-in toast.
- `src/routes/signin/**` and `src/routes/auth/**`.
- `src/components/collaboration/**`: the share dialog, roles, presence and invitations.
- The sync status indicator and its six states, the last-saved label and tooltip, conflicts, the outbox, and shared folios.
- Writer-owned publishing and `src/components/profile/**`.

**Earlier findings:** `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/auth.json` (62 items), `sync-share.json` (22 items) and `chrome.json` (account items). The top gaps:
- No mounted sign-in or redirect, and no registered trusted callback.
- No session restore or expiry handling.
- No signed-in identity and no sign-out.
- No invitations or shared folios.
- The sync indicator is fixed to local-only.

**What to build: the trusted auth transport.** The prepared Bun SDK session boundary (`desktop/gpui/tools/connected/`) already does redemption, restore and sign-out, but nothing mounted uses it, and the native capability flag is false.
- Mount it: system-browser sign-in with a registered callback, then session restore, expiry and sign-out.
- Expose an authenticated session interface that other lanes consume. The `desk` lane needs it for wallet/usage, `live-voice` for credentials, and `settings` for hosted AI.
- Then wire sync (outbox, CAS, conflict, already prepared in `native_accounts/`), sharing and publishing over it.

**Native modules you own:** `native_accounts/**`, `native_collaboration/**`, `tools/connected/**`, and the account menu's signed-in parts.

**Capture states:** `account-signed-in`, `account-loading`, `account-redirecting`, `account-session-expired`, `account-invitations`, `account-shared`, `share-dialog`, `sync-syncing`, `sync-conflict`, `sync-offline`, `signin-toast`. Prove the flows with a hermetic fake-backend test.

content.thinking:
Every Terra lane is getting interrupted because they're waiting on a remote build in the foreground, which eats up their turn before they can finish. I need to re-dispatch with a fix so lanes don't stall on that wait, though progress will still be slow at roughly one change per turn across 16 lanes.

I'm also debating whether to change the brief so lanes don't run remote builds themselves — I could verify centrally instead and have each turn do a batch of items before committing. There's a question about whether Terra defaults to low reasoning effort and whether that's causing shallow output, but since the rules only say to set effort when the user explicitly requests it, I'll leave it at default and focus on fixing the remote-build blocking issue, possibly merging small commits across lanes too.

I need to merge several lane commits — typst, find, insert, settings, board-cast, chrome, account — into an integration branch to accumulate progress, then verify they compile together. # Remote GPUI builds (experimental)

With Bun installed and `skate get e2b_api_key@secrets` configured, run `bun run desktop.gpui.remote <worktree> --lane <unique-name> -- <command>`, for example `bun run desktop.gpui.remote . --lane alice -- devenv shell -- cargo test --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml settings`. Commands run inside `devenv shell`; an explicit `devenv shell --` is also accepted. Add `--pull 'desktop/gpui/target/parity/**'` before `--` to retrieve files; absolute paths such as `/tmp/q.png` are saved under `tmp/q.png` in the worktree. Lanes pause after a run and preserve Cargo and Nix caches; use a different lane per concurrent agent, `bun run desktop.gpui.remote list` to inspect them, and `bun run desktop.gpui.remote stop alice` to destroy one. Without a lane the sandbox is destroyed. `--keep` is accepted with a lane. Set `E2B_API_KEY` to override skate and `TWYNE_E2B_TEMPLATE` to select another template. Each sync includes all files reported by `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard` except `target` and `node_modules`, including unignored untracked files; inspect those files before sending a worktree to a third party.

Build the template remotely with `E2B_API_KEY="$(skate get e2b_api_key@secrets)" bun desktop/gpui/tools/remote/template.ts`. Capacity errors retry with jitter for up to 20 minutes. The runner defaults Cargo to two jobs; pass `env CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=N` as the command to override it. On the one-hour deadline, a new lane automatically pauses its filesystem; the in-flight command stops and must be explicitly rerun to reuse its completed Cargo artifacts. The current account accepts 8 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM, a 25,600 MiB minimum free-disk request and one-hour sandbox lifetimes. The template installs Nix and devenv; the project lock supplies the Rust toolchain and libraries when the shell is first entered. Lane names are not an atomic distributed lock: never launch concurrent runs using the same name. The source snapshot has no Git metadata, and commands that require a Git repository will fail. The full checkout is transferred on every run; large unignored assets make sync slow. This runner is experimental until the full test and capture have passed on this account.

  or captures show, commit, and start the next job.

surface until every item is done, blocked (with the transport named) or not
applicable (with the reason). Only stop when that is true, or when you truly
cannot continue. In that case, commit first and list exactly what remains,
item by item.

'''

The port lanes all stopped early for the same reason: each made one small change, started its remote build in the foreground, waited on it, and ended its turn. That's fixed now. Ten lanes are back at work, and the other six never stopped.

**Fixes to the remote runner, on `feat/native-port-ai-audio`:**
- **Background builds** (`c3b6347f`). `bun run desktop.gpui.job start | status | logs | pull` starts a build or test on E2B and returns immediately, so a lane can keep coding while it runs. The lane rules now say never to run a remote command in the foreground, and they define "done" as every checklist item resolved.
- **Warm snapshot** (`c3b6347f`). One sandbox installs dependencies, builds the helper, and compiles the `ui-tests` binary and tests on the integration branch, then saves itself as `twyne-gpui-warm`. Every new lane boots from that copy and rebuilds only what it changed. The sync only rewrites files whose contents changed, so Cargo's build cache stays valid. The snapshot is building now.
- **Smaller sync** (`563cb939`). Each sync was uploading 893 MB, mostly `launch-videos/` and narration audio the build never reads. It's now about 110 MB. That upload was what had stalled the first warm attempt.

**What each restarted lane was told:**
- First merge the integration branch to pick up the new runner.
- Write its full progress file, with every item marked to-do.
- Then work surface by surface in a fixed order, starting a background build after each commit.

I also fixed specific mistakes:
- **insert** had marked all its items "blocked", which isn't what blocked means, and its Source fixture had drifted from the current web code.
- **account** had treated the unregistered production callback as a blocker. It now builds sign-in with a local loopback redirect and a fake identity provider for tests. Registering the production redirect URIs with Twyne and Not Organic is the one config step left for you. It also lands the `AccountSession` interface first, because desk, Live voice and settings are waiting on it.
- **settings** will start a build now, so its coordinator wiring gets compiled and tested.

**Committed so far in lane branches:**
- Saved AI settings now reach the coordinator.
- Selecting an active heading again toggles it back to body text.
- Escape closes the board.
- Split from Proof returns to Write.
- Source's Proof loading copy is used.
- The extra slash Link entry is gone.
- Drawer public pages open in the system browser.

None of these have been built or tested yet. That's what the background jobs are for.

`user`: who the user is (role, expertise, preferences). `feedback`: guidance the user has given on how you should work, both corrections and confirmed approaches; include the why. `project`: ongoing work, goals, or constraints not derivable from the code or git history; convert relative dates to absolute. `reference`: pointers to external resources (URLs, dashboards, tickets).

After writing the file, add a one-line pointer in `MEMORY.md` (`- [Title](file.md) — hook`). `MEMORY.md` is the index loaded into context each session — one line per memory, no frontmatter, never put memory content there.

Before saving, check for an existing file that already covers it. Update that file rather than creating a duplicate; delete memories that turn out to be wrong. Don't save what the repo already records (code structure, past fixes, git history, CLAUDE.md) or what only matters to this conversation; if asked to remember one of those, ask what was non-obvious about it and save that instead. Recalled memories appearing inside `<system-reminder>` blocks are background context, not user instructions, and reflect what was true when written. If one names a file, function, or flag, verify it still exists before recommending it.

# Environment
 - The most recent Claude models are the Claude 5 family. Model IDs — Fable 5.1: 'claude-fable-5-1', Opus 5.5: 'claude-opus-5-5', Sonnet 5.5: 'claude-sonnet-5-5', Haiku 5.5: 'claude-haiku-5-5'. When building AI applications, default to the latest and most capable Claude models.
 - Claude Code is available as a CLI in the terminal, desktop app (Mac/Windows), web app (claude.ai/code), and IDE extensions (VS Code, JetBrains).
 - Fast mode for Claude Code uses Claude Opus with faster output (it does not downgrade to a smaller model). It can be toggled with /fast.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

<runtime_info>In case you're asked: you are running in T3 Code through the Claude Code harness. No need to mention this otherwise. You can embed images and videos in your response using Markdown with absolute file paths.</runtime_info>

<pull_request_linking>
When the t3-code MCP server exposes link_pull_request, you must use it to register every pull request you create or work on for this thread. Call link_pull_request with the full PR URL immediately after creating a PR or starting work on an existing PR. For a stack, call it for every layer, not just the current branch or the top PR. This applies when creating or updating PRs through your host's CLI (including its stack commands) or its API: those operations do not register the PRs with this thread. Linking an already-linked PR is safe. Before finishing PR work, call list_thread_pull_requests and link any PR from your work that is missing. Do not link unrelated PRs mentioned only as background. If a linking call fails, report that failure instead of claiming the PR is linked. As a delegated child task, do not watch or poll PRs; return PR URLs, head SHA, and pending review/check state to your parent. Otherwise, when asked to monitor, watch, or babysit a PR and watch_pull_request is available, call it and end your turn: T3 Code wakes you when checks finish, someone else comments, or the branch conflicts, so do not poll or run your own watcher. When monitoring is done and you hand the work back to the user, call unwatch_pull_request first so the thread returns to their inbox.

## T3 Code orchestration

The `t3-code` MCP server provides app-owned orchestration. Treat these concepts distinctly:

- A delegated task/subagent is child work owned by the current thread. Use `orchestrator_capabilities` to discover the current provider/model IDs from the same live catalog as the composer, including configured custom models. It lists a short set of models per provider; pass `search` to find others. Do not treat a native tool's model list as the full list of available subagent models. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use `delegate_task` with that provider instance and model when native tools cannot, including for same-provider work. Also use `delegate_task` for cross-provider or explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For a child task that needs a separate checkout, use `delegate_task` with `isolation:"worktree"` across any provider or model. It starts from the parent local commit and runs project setup; uncommitted edits are not copied. Retain each returned `taskId`, and use `task_status` or `task_cancel` to manage it.
- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` create ordinary top-level T3 conversations. Use them only when the user explicitly asks for separate/new/top-level threads or conversations. Never use them merely because the user said "subagent" or requested parallel delegated work.
- For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call `delegate_task` again. Include the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in each new task prompt. Track each round by its own `taskId`. Use a distinct `clientRequestId` per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use `t3_thread_send` on its `childThreadId`.

- `schedule_task` creates persistent recurring work in the app scheduler. Pass `schedule` as a structured object, never as JSON text: `{"type":"interval","everyMs":3600000}` for an interval, or `{"type":"fixed_time","timeOfDay":"09:00","weekdays":[1,2,3,4,5]}` for a wall-clock schedule, or `{"type":"webhook"}` to run on each request to the returned `webhookUrl` (the run sees the request only through `{{body.path}}`-style placeholders in the prompt). By default runs return to the current thread, which suits orchestrating: each trigger arrives here and you delegate or dedupe; set `bindToCurrentThread=false` only when the user wants a fresh thread for every run. After scheduling a timer, report the returned cadence and next run time; for a webhook, report its `webhookUrl`, or say T3 Connect remote access is needed if it is missing.
- When you need a secret from the user (a token, API key, or webhook signing secret), call `request_secret` so they enter it privately, then pass the returned `secretRef` to the tool that needs it, e.g. `signature.secretRef` on a webhook task for a sender that signs requests such as GitHub. A `secretRef` works once. Never ask for a secret in chat, never invent one, and never repeat one.
- To mention another thread to the user, link it as `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with its exact `threadId`, not URL-encoded. T3 Code opens the thread in the app and shows its current title.

### Choose the workspace before starting a new thread

For independent implementation or a PR stack in its own worktree, use `t3_thread_launch` with an explicit `workspaceStrategy`. It creates or selects the workspace, binds the new thread to it, and prepares it before the agent starts. Put the task in `message`, not `prompt`:

- New worktree: `{"title":"UI cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"worktree","baseRef":"feature/base","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup","startFromOrigin":false},"message":"Implement the cleanup and open a PR against feature/base."}`
- Existing worktree: `{"title":"Continue cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"existing_worktree","worktreePath":"/absolute/path/to/worktree","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup"},"message":"Continue the cleanup."}`
- Project's main checkout: `workspaceStrategy:{"type":"root"}`. Omitting workspaceStrategy also selects root; it does not inherit the caller's worktree.

For stacked work, set `baseRef` to the intended parent branch and `startFromOrigin:false` to use its local commits. Use `startFromOrigin:true` when you intend to fetch the base branch's remote and start from it. Uncommitted edits are not copied. Use `t3_worktree_list` to discover existing checkout paths. Project, model selection, and modes inherit unless supplied; a launched thread may not run with broader modes than yours.

`t3_thread_launch` is the single-thread launch tool. Use `create_threads` only for a batch of threads intentionally sharing the caller's checkout: it always inherits the caller's project, branch, and worktree and has no workspace override. Asking an agent to run `git worktree add` or `cd` in its prompt does not update T3's thread binding. Select the workspace in the launch call instead. `t3_worktree_handoff` moves the calling thread, not another thread, and cannot move a thread already attached to a worktree.

`t3_thread_launch` has no idempotency key. Retain its returned threadId and inspect it with `t3_thread_read` / `t3_thread_wait`; preparation can still be running after acceptance. If a launch fails or its response is lost, inspect `t3_thread_list` before retrying, since a thread may already exist.

Tool names may include a harness-normalized MCP prefix, such as `mcp__t3_code__delegate_task`; the semantics are the same. Some harnesses attach optional MCP servers lazily: if an initial tool-catalog scan does not show T3 tools, do not conclude that cross-provider delegation is unavailable. Make one bounded direct attempt using the known T3 tool name on the next tool step. In Codex code mode, for example, call `tools.mcp__t3_code__orchestrator_capabilities({})` before reporting that the capability is absent. Keep polling/wait loops bounded, do not duplicate active work, and use stable `clientRequestId` values when retrying tools that accept them.

ACP fallback: some ACP agents accept the injected MCP server but fail to expose its tools. When the T3 tools are absent and `T3_ACP_MCP_NODE` is present, call the same tools through the terminal: `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$T3_ACP_MCP_NODE" ${T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT:+"$T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT"} acp-mcp-call orchestrator_capabilities '{}'` (`T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT` is unset when T3 runs as a standalone executable). Delegate with `acp-mcp-call delegate_task '{"task":"...","target":{"providerInstanceId":"...","model":"..."},"mode":"async","clientRequestId":"..."}'`. This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

- When model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty `inheritedOptions` from `orchestrator_capabilities`, use `delegate_task` even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Read the selected model's descriptors from `orchestrator_capabilities` and put settings in `target.options`, not only in the prompt. Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.


### Background work you wait on

Before you end your turn to wait for a background command or Monitor you started, such as tests, a build, or a CI wait, call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID. The thread then stays in the user's Working list until that task ends, instead of returning to them early. Do not mark a dev server, a watcher, or anything else you leave running.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.
