tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__delegate_task
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Delegate one task to a T3-owned child agent/subagent of THIS thread and run it with only the supplied task prompt, without copying parent conversation history. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use t3_thread_send on its childThreadId. Set isolation to worktree for a separate checkout based on the parent local commit, with project setup completed before the child starts. Uncommitted edits are not copied; omitted isolation shares the parent checkout. Use delegate_task when model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty inheritedOptions from orchestrator_capabilities, even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Set target.options using advertised IDs: Claude {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Check providerInstanceId, model, and options in the result. Provider/model and modes inherit unless overridden. Options inherit only for the same instance and model; explicit entries override individual values and [] or {} clears them. A requested runtimeMode must be one the target provider lists in orchestrator_capabilities runtimeModes; an inherited one steps down to the broadest mode it offers. Leave runtimeMode unset unless the user asks for a supervised child: approval-required and auto-accept-edits usually make the child wait for a person at each action that needs approval. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion, a blocking question, a pending approval, or timeout. If hasPendingQuestion, pass threadId=childThreadId to t3_pending_request_list, t3_pending_request_read (with requestId) and t3_pending_request_respond, or ask the user; the task's completion still wakes this thread. If pendingApproval is set, read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback. It grants no approval authority; decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder, and pending request tools answer questions only. The child keeps running and its completion still wakes this thread. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

anyOf.description: Model options from orchestrator_capabilities. For the same provider instance and model, overrides individual inherited values; [] or {} clears them. Claude: {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex: {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Only use options advertised by the selected model.
Defaults to shared: use the parent's checkout. Worktree creates a separate checkout from the parent's current local commit before starting the child. Uncommitted edits are not copied.

Defaults to async. Use wait only when this turn needs the child's result before you can continue. A blocking question or a pending approval in the child ends the wait early with the task still running.

timeoutMs.description: Wait budget for mode=wait only. Default 10 minutes. Elapsing it returns waitTimedOut=true on that call and does not cancel the child.

anyOf.description: Defaults to inherit; omit it unless the user asks for a supervised child. A narrower mode is not a read-only switch: on most providers, approval-required and auto-accept-edits pause the child at each action that needs approval until a person approves it in the child's thread, which this thread cannot do. To limit what the child does, say so in the task. A mode ranked above this thread's is rejected; that ranking does not promise the child's provider permissions are narrower than this thread's.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__orchestrator_capabilities
tools.description: List the V2 provider instances, a short list of their models from the same live catalog as the composer, inherited runtime settings, and app-owned orchestration features available to this caller. The list has the user's favorite and custom models, your own model, every current Codex, Claude, Muse and Grok model, and the first 8 current models of other providers. Other legacy models are left out. omittedModels counts models left out; pass search, such as 'sonnet 4.6', to find them. delegate_task accepts any catalog model, listed or not. For a separate top-level thread in a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_background_wait
tools.description: Keep this thread in the user's Working list and out of their inbox while you wait for background work. Start a background command or Monitor first. Call this before you end your turn if you will act on its result when it wakes you. In taskIds, give the ID shown when the task started. The thread stays in Working until the task ends. The user is not told the work is done. Do not mark work you leave running, such as a dev server or watcher. Unmarked commands and monitors never keep the thread in Working. Pass waiting=false to remove the mark. This does not stop the task. IDs that are not running return in unmatched and change nothing. Only Claude threads support this tool. Other providers return an error.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_send
tools.description: Send a message to any T3 thread in this environment. The target cannot have broader permission modes than the caller. Use delegate_task with the full review context and a new clientRequestId for independent review rounds. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, send to its childThreadId. After the original task completes, a requested follow-up creates a fresh task in that child thread and returns taskId when it starts a turn or restarts a turn without its own task; its completion notifies the parent, and the original result stays unchanged. A steer that joins a running turn returns that turn's task, if it has one. mode='auto' starts an idle thread, steers a fully active turn, or queues behind a turn that is not yet steerable. Use queue for a separate follow-up turn, steer for an in-flight update, or restart to interrupt-and-restart the active turn. clientRequestId makes retries idempotent.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__task_status
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Read a T3-owned delegated task created by this parent thread. childRunId identifies the original delegated run. workState distinguishes working, waiting_for_children, and result_available; a completed turn with live nested work is not a completed task. summary is the final task result, including provider errors on failure, and remains stable after publication. hasPendingChildRuns reports later queued or executing turns in the backing child thread, even after the task is terminal; it does not reopen the task, and task_cancel stops those turns too. Turns held in a stopped queue wait for the user and do not count. latestTerminal* provides later non-monitor turn results; latestTerminalSummary and latestTerminalResultContextTransferId are independently null when they exactly repeat summary and resultContextTransferId, respectively. pendingApproval identifies the oldest pending live approval for this task's own unfinished work. Read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback and grants no approval authority. Decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder. Reading a terminal result acknowledges its automatic parent delivery.

The full desktop isn't at parity with the browser yet. All 16 port lanes are working again, and lanes are finally landing real commits. But nothing has been built or tested remotely yet, and no surface has a pixel score.

The lanes kept stopping after one small change for three reasons:
- **Commits hung.** `devenv shell -- git commit` never finished. The commit hook was pointing at a `prek` binary that no longer exists in the Nix store. I linked a current one into `~/.local/bin`, so plain `git commit` now passes the hook in about a second.
- **Remote jobs died.** The background-job command I'd written stayed tied to the request that started it, so it timed out. Jobs now use E2B's own background mode (`2ca0f85c`).
- **Key lookups collided.** Several lanes reading the E2B key from `skate` at once hit its database lock. The key is now read from a private cache file (`~/.config/twyne/e2b_api_key`, readable only by you), with `skate` as the fallback.

I told every lane to merge the fixes and commit with plain `git`. The four lanes that had stopped with uncommitted work were sent back to commit it first.

**Real progress in lane branches** (none built or tested yet):
- **Settings:** a checklist, removal that cancels when focus leaves, and saved AI settings connected to the coordinator.
- **Narration:** a player API with commands and queues, and playback tracked from the audio device.
- **Board-cast:** Escape closes the board, with a test.
- **Smaller fixes:** heading toggle-back, Split from Proof returning to Write, Proof loading copy, removal of the extra slash Link entry, and drawer public pages opening in the system browser.
- **Live voice:** a credential interface and handshake are staged. It found that LFM3-Audio doesn't have the realtime WebSocket API in `llama-server` yet. So the local Live option is built behind an interface and will show "not available on this device" until a runtime provides it.

**Building now:** the warm snapshot on E2B, the shared build that new lanes start from. Once it finishes, a lane's first remote build only recompiles what it changed.

**One thing you'll need to do:** the account lane is building sign-in with a local loopback redirect, so it doesn't need production setup to work. The production redirect URIs still have to be registered with Twyne and Not Organic. I'll give you the exact URIs when that lane lands.

These builds are all cold, running from 02:08 to 02:19, with dependency counts ranging widely. Comparing timing against the warm build that finished around 02:18 after roughly 30 minutes at 6 jobs, I'm estimating that cold builds at only 2 jobs could take 60-90 minutes, which would exceed the 1-hour job lifetime and cause them to pause or stop on timeout.

With warm cache, only the twyne-desktop crate needs rebuilding since the vendored gpui crates stay unchanged, making each rebuild much faster — maybe 3-5 minutes. I'm checking that mtimes work correctly: since syncWorktree only touches changed files, only twyne-desktop should get new timestamps and need recompiling, and the absolute path stays consistent so Cargo fingerprints hold. I'm deciding to set CARGO_BUILD_JOBS to 6 for lanes since the warm build succeeded at that level including linking the test binaries, and now I'm considering killing the cold sandboxes to restart from the warm state instead.

Rather than making lanes restart manually, the cleanest approach is to transparently migrate each lane myself: read its run.sh and pulls.json, kill the cold sandbox, spin up a new one from the warm snapshot, sync that lane's worktree, and relaunch the same command so status just shows it running on the new sandbox. I'm now mapping each lane name to its corresponding branch and worktree path so I know exactly what to sync and restart for each one.

Simplest approach is to just copy the existing run.sh and job config verbatim into the new sandbox rather than reconstructing the launch command by hand.

I'm planning a restart-warm.ts script: for each lane, kill the current sandbox, spin up a fresh one from the warm template, sync the worktree, then write back the same job files and restart the job in the background, reusing the startJob logic inline. I also want to bump default parallel jobs to 6 since that worked fine on warm, though I'm wary of memory spikes when lanes link multiple test binaries in parallel.

Each test binary link takes a few GB, so 6 parallel links could risk an 8GB OOM, but since warm already succeeded with 6 on this same workload, I'll stick with 6 rather than dropping to 4. I also want to confirm the lane sandbox's hour-long timeout with pause-on-timeout is enough for a warm rebuild, then figure out how worktrees map to lanes.

All 15 lanes booted cold and are compiling too slowly to finish before E2B's one-hour sandbox limit. I'll quietly migrate each lane to a warm snapshot by syncing its worktree and re-queuing its job on a fresh sandbox, starting with getting the lane-to-worktree mapping.

content.thinking:
The user wants Railway instead of E2B for remote execution, likely due to cost or preference. I need to figure out what switching entails — whether to halt active E2B sandboxes immediately given they're currently in use by the lanes.

My plan is to build a Railway backend that matches the same job interface so lanes don't need command changes, then phase out E2B once Railway's confirmed working. Since lanes are designed to never block on a runner failure, stopping E2B now and routing job.ts to refuse E2B or redirect to Railway seems reasonable, though I need to think through whether Railway's PaaS model can even support the kind of arbitrary sandboxed execution E2B provides.

I'm weighing options: deploy a worker service on Railway exposing an HTTP API that accepts a tarball, runs a command, streams logs, and returns artifacts, backed by a cargo cache volume. Railway's Pro plan actually offers far more resources than E2B — up to 32 vCPU/32GB per service and 50GB volumes — and the CLI's `railway ssh` could let me exec commands directly into a running container, so I'm considering whether to run one large worker or multiple smaller services per lane given 16 lanes building concurrently.

Cost-wise, Railway charges roughly $0.028/vCPU-hr and $0.014/GB-hr, so an 8vCPU/16GB worker runs about $0.45/hr, comparable to E2B. For the design, I'm sketching a worker image with Nix/devenv plus a lightweight Bun HTTP job server exposing sync, job, status, logs, and pull endpoints, authenticated via a shared secret, with the Nix store itself needing to live on the persistent volume since it's large and costly to rebuild each time.

Since a volume can only mount one path, I'd mount it at /data, point CARGO_TARGET_DIR there, and bake the devenv toolchain into the image at build time by running the shell setup against the repo's devenv config. Cold builds per worker would take roughly 30 minutes at low concurrency but drop to around 10 minutes with more vCPUs, and I'm now weighing how many workers to run — likely one per lane, each with its own persistent volume.

Per-lane services avoid cache contention but I need to check Railway's limits on services per project and whether I should deploy via a shared image pushed to a registry versus building from the repo's Dockerfile directly. I'm also unsure what plan the user is on, so I should check their account details before committing to a 16-service architecture.

Given how central this runner infrastructure is, I'm weighing whether to build it myself or delegate to a Terra lane with a tight spec — Terra lanes have stalled before, but the remote runner lane previously delivered well, so delegation seems viable. Meanwhile I should figure out what to do about E2B: the user wants Railway instead, so I need to stop spinning up new E2B sandboxes without leaving lanes without any remote execution option in the interim.

I'll make `job start` return a message that the remote runner is moving to Railway, telling lanes to keep coding with local checks in the meantime. Running E2B sandboxes cost compute so I'll kill them now, but I'll keep the warm snapshot around cheaply until Railway is confirmed working, even though killing sandboxes mid-flight will disrupt lanes' in-progress jobs.

Now I need to look into Railway's capabilities — checking if there's SSH access via CLI, what the help output shows, and what the volume size limits and plan constraints look like.

input.content:
# Remote GPUI builds

Desktop builds, tests and captures run on Railway sandboxes in the
`twyne-gpui-builds` project. Each port lane has its own sandbox and runs
detached jobs, so an agent can start a build and keep working:

```sh
bun run desktop.gpui.job start . --lane <lane> --pull 'desktop/gpui/target/parity/**' -- <command...>
bun run desktop.gpui.job status <lane>          # running | finished N | interrupted | none
bun run desktop.gpui.job logs <lane> --lines 80 # tail of the output
bun run desktop.gpui.job pull . --lane <lane>   # copy --pull files and remote-job.log back
bun run desktop.gpui.job stop <lane>            # destroy the lane's sandbox
bun run desktop.gpui.job list                   # lanes and their sandboxes
```

## How it works

- **Running commands.** Commands run inside `devenv shell` in `/root/work`,
  so they use the pinned toolchain.
- **Syncing.** Each `start` streams the worktree's tracked and unignored files
  in. Launch videos and audio are left out. Files are compared by content, so
  unchanged files keep their timestamps and Cargo rebuilds only what the lane
  edited.
- **Checkpoints.** New lanes boot from the `twyne-gpui-warm` checkpoint. It
  already has dependencies installed, the document helper built, and the
  `ui-tests` binary and tests compiled.
  - Rebuild it after large changes on the integration branch with
    `bun desktop/gpui/tools/remote/railway.ts warm <worktree>`.
  - `twyne-gpui-base` holds just the toolchain: the apt libraries, Nix and
    devenv 2.4.0.
- **Lane records** live in `~/.config/twyne/railway-lanes.json`.
- **Idle timeout.** Sandboxes are destroyed after 120 idle minutes, so stop
  your lane when done.

The E2B runner (`run.ts`, `job.ts`, `warm.ts`, `rewarm.ts`) is retired and
refuses to start jobs.

Use detached jobs to build and test without blocking:

```sh
bun run desktop.gpui.job list                   # lanes and their sandboxes
```

## How it works

- **Running commands.** Commands run inside `devenv shell` in `/root/work`,
  so they use the pinned toolchain.
- **Syncing.** Each `start` streams the worktree's tracked and unignored files
  in. Launch videos and audio are left out. Files are compared by content, so
  unchanged files keep their timestamps and Cargo rebuilds only what the lane
  edited.
- **Checkpoints.** New lanes boot from the `twyne-gpui-warm` checkpoint. It
  already has dependencies installed, the document helper built, and the
  `ui-tests` binary and tests compiled.
  - Rebuild it after large changes on the integration branch with
    `bun desktop/gpui/tools/remote/railway.ts warm <worktree>`.
  - `twyne-gpui-base` holds just the toolchain: the apt libraries, Nix and
    devenv 2.4.0.
- **Lane records** live in `~/.config/twyne/railway-lanes.json`.
- **Idle timeout.** Sandboxes are destroyed after 120 idle minutes, so stop
  your lane when done.

The E2B runner (`run.ts`, `job.ts`, `warm.ts`, `rewarm.ts`) is retired and
refuses to start jobs.

content.text:
I've switched remote builds to Railway, and E2B is fully shut down. I stopped all 16 E2B sandboxes, and the old E2B runner now refuses to start jobs, so none can start again by accident.

The new runner is `desktop/gpui/tools/remote/railway.ts` (commit `e1fe8fcf` on `feat/native-port-ai-audio`). Lanes keep using the same commands (`bun run desktop.gpui.job start | status | logs | pull | stop | list`), so their briefs didn't need rewriting.

- **Project:** a new, separate Railway project, `twyne-gpui-builds`, so these sandboxes stay apart from your live services. Each sandbox has 8 vCPU, 7 GB RAM and 29 GB disk.
- **Checkpoints:** `twyne-gpui-base` is saved and holds the toolchain: system libraries, Nix and devenv 2.4.0. `twyne-gpui-warm` adds dependencies, the document helper, and the built `ui-tests` binary and tests. It's building now, and every lane will boot from it once it's ready.
- **Jobs:** each lane gets its own sandbox. A job starts in the background and returns immediately, and syncing only rewrites changed files. A sandbox is destroyed after 120 idle minutes.
- **Checked so far:** upload, download and detached runs all work on a real sandbox. A test job got as far as entering the project's devenv shell.

Two Railway quirks the runner works around:
- Commands run without `$USER` set, so Nix doesn't load until the runner sets `USER=root`.
- The `--project` and `--environment` flags have to come before `--`, otherwise they become part of the command.

Railway labels sandboxes as experimental, and its template builder fails without saying which step failed. So I set up the toolchain inside a live sandbox and saved it as a checkpoint instead.

All 16 lanes have been told to merge the switch. Most picked it up mid-turn, and the idle ones will get it at the start of their next turn. Until the warm checkpoint exists, a lane's first job builds from scratch, so they're starting jobs and carrying on coding. I've also updated memory: Railway is the preferred remote runner, along with these setup details.

The first attempt at the shared warm build on Railway failed before it compiled anything. Railway's command relay (`ssh.railway.com:2226`) timed out while the job was starting, which looks like a temporary connection fault on their side. The runner now retries when it can't reach the relay (`b21cc1c7`), and the warm build is running again.

**Lane jobs are already running on Railway.** Six lanes have live sandboxes: settings, exchange, inflow, typst-views, chrome, and the warm build itself. Until the warm checkpoint is ready, those lanes compile from scratch.

**Lanes are porting real behaviour now:**
- **Typst views:** the Source draft banner now sits above all the panes, so it stays visible in Write, Source and Proof. The visual editor stays read-only while a draft is pending, which matches how the web version behaves.
- **Instruments:** the native Sentence Lab is an older card, while the web version is now a much larger Sentence Bench. The lane is fixing a behaviour gap first: native accepts unfinished or stale wording. It will then rebuild the bench to match.

The "cancelled" messages from those two lanes were older turns, replaced when I sent the Railway switch. Both lanes are still running.

I'll report when the warm checkpoint is ready, and as lanes land commits and pixel scores.

The desktop isn't at parity with the browser yet, and no surface has a pixel score so far. The 16 port lanes are now committing steadily, but none of that work has been built or tested yet, so every checklist still shows 0 items done.

**Biggest commit runs this round:**
- **Desk** (about 20 commits): My Desk now opens a native desk with local writing activity, pace and recent work. Writer patterns and a forecast line are partly done, and you can delete the local activity record after confirming.
- **Typst views** (about 20 commits): Source draft and save-error alerts, proof zoom and PDF controls, Split keeping its mode when you switch workspaces, and Zen and Split capture states.
- **Instruments** (about 19 commits): the Sentence Bench, with wording checks and comparison, candidate sources, and context.
- **Dossier** (14 commits): starter documents now match the web's title-only version. Format suggestions now list every match and have the chevron.
- **Editor input** (10 commits): double-click and triple-click selection with drag, more shortcuts, and tests for undo grouping and typing non-ASCII characters.
- **Live voice** (8 commits): a hosted connection over a websocket (new crate: `tungstenite`) with a fake-gateway test, a signed-out desk the Talk button opens, and audio, transcript and delegation pieces that aren't connected to each other yet.

**Conflict fix** (`dbe11e30`). Before merging anything, I test-merged all 16 lane branches. Nine collided on the same three hard-coded lists of capture-state names. Each lane now keeps its own list in `tools/parity/states.d/<lane>.json`, and the native check and harness read the base list plus all of those. A few conflicts remain in `app.rs`, `room_layout.rs` and `Cargo.lock`, between live-voice, account and desk. I've asked those lanes to keep their host edits in one marked block each, so I can resolve them mechanically when I merge.

**"Blocked" items that weren't real blockers.** Lanes kept marking work as blocked when it was really their own job: settings marked language as blocked on native locale support, and dossier marked the conversation's host connection. I've told every lane that "blocked" means only something outside this repo, like a production registration. Anything native they build themselves.

**Builds on Railway.** About 11 lane sandboxes are compiling from scratch, and the warm checkpoint build restarted at 02:50 UTC. Once it's saved, new lane sandboxes start from it, so they only rebuild what changed. I'll merge each lane into the integration branch once its remote tests pass, so lanes can use each other's work: Cast speech calling the narration player, and desk, Live voice and hosted AI using the account session.

"""Resolve conflict hunks from the capture-state blocks in shared host files.

Handles three shapes, refusing anything else:
- both sides only added code at the same spot: keep ours, then theirs;
- ours added blocks next to an unchanged base line that theirs edited:
  keep our additions with their edit of that line;
- the mirror of that."""
import re, sys
path = sys.argv[1]
s = open(path).read()
pat = re.compile(r'<<<<<<< [^\n]*\n(.*?)(?:\|\|\|\|\|\|\| [^\n]*\n(.*?))?=======\n(.*?)>>>>>>> [^\n]*\n', re.S)
bad = []
def fix(m):
    ours, base, theirs = m.group(1), m.group(2) or "", m.group(3)
    if not base.strip():
        return ours + theirs
    if ours.endswith(base):
        return ours[: -len(base)] + theirs
    if ours.startswith(base):
        return theirs + ours[len(base):]
    if theirs.endswith(base):
        return theirs[: -len(base)] + ours
    if theirs.startswith(base):
        return ours + theirs[len(base):]
    bad.append(m.group(0)[:400]); return m.group(0)
n = len(pat.findall(s))
out = pat.sub(fix, s)
open(path, "w").write(out)
print(f"{path}: {n} hunks, {n - len(bad)} resolved")
for b in bad: print("UNRESOLVED:\n" + b + "\n...")
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
EOF

You go past a row of houses and it is still there, over the roofs. You go round a corner and it comes too. The trees whip past, the lamp posts whip past, and the moon just hangs there, keeping up, as if it has nothing better to do.

It is not following you. It only looks that way, and the reason is one of the best tricks your eyes play on you.

Here is the trick. Hold your thumb up at arm's length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps. Now look at something across the room and do the same thing. It jumps less. Now look out of the window at the furthest thing you can see. It barely moves at all. The further away something is, the less it seems to move when you move. The moon is very, very far away, so far that when the car goes a whole mile, the moon has moved, from your point of view, by nothing you could notice. The houses are close, so they rush past. The moon is far, so it stays. That is the whole trick.

The apparent angular displacement of a distant object under lateral translation of the observer is inversely proportional to its distance, a phenomenon generally termed motion parallax, and the lunar case represents the limiting condition in which the parallax angle approaches zero.

The moon does something else that is strange, and this one even grown-ups argue about. When it is low down, just coming up over the houses, it looks huge. An hour later, high in the sky, it looks small. If you hold out your thumb and cover it, you will find your thumb covers it both times, exactly the same. It has not changed size. Your brain has changed its mind about how big it is.

Nobody is completely sure why. The best guess is this. When the moon is low, you see it next to things you know the size of: houses, trees, a church. Your brain says, that is as big as a house, and that is far away, so it must be enormous. When the moon is high, there is nothing next to it, just sky, and your brain has nothing to compare it with, so it decides the moon is small. Same moon. Different neighbours.

Contemporary accounts invoke a conjunction of the Ponzo illusion and size-distance invariance, though the literature remains unsettled, and it is doubtful that any single explanatory model will prove adequate to the full phenomenology of the effect.

You can test this. Next time the moon is low and looks huge, bend over and look at it upside down between your legs. It will look smaller. Nothing has changed except that your brain can no longer line it up with the houses, so it stops pretending.

So here is what to tell the grown-up in the front seat. Hold up your thumb. Close one eye, then the other. Show them how the thumb jumps and the far-off thing does not. Then tell them the moon is the furthest-off thing there is, so it does not jump at all, which is why it seems to keep up with the car. Then, if the moon is low, tell them to bend over and look at it upside down. They will not want to. Make them. It works.

The moon is about two hundred and forty thousand miles away. That is so far that if you drove there at motorway speed, without stopping, it would take you about five months. The car has gone one mile. The moon has noticed nothing. It is not following you. It is just too far away to be left behind.

And one more thing for the ride home. The stars do the same trick, and they are so much further away that they do not even seem to move when the whole planet turns underneath them for an hour. For as long as there has been a Harbour Ward, there has been a question about what to do with the food we do not eat. The ward's first refuse collection began in 1894, with a horse-drawn cart and two men who were paid in part with the right to sell what they collected. Kitchen scraps went to pig keepers on the edge of town, and for sixty years that arrangement, informal as it was, meant that very little of the ward's food waste ended up in the ground.

That changed in the 1950s, when the pig keepers were moved out and the council introduced the bins most of us still use. Since then, almost all food waste in the ward has gone to landfill, where it breaks down without air and produces methane, a gas that warms the planet many times more effectively than carbon dioxide. The council's most recent waste audit found that food makes up roughly a third of what goes into the average Harbour Ward bin by weight.

Across the country, councils have begun separating food waste for collection, and the results have been encouraging. Food collected separately can be processed in sealed digesters that capture the methane and burn it for electricity, and what remains can be spread on farmland. The ward's waste team has been studying these schemes for two years, visiting four other councils and reviewing the costs, and we have come to the view that a separate food-waste collection would work here.

We are therefore running a pilot. Four hundred households in the streets between the harbour and the railway line, including yours, have been selected. Households that take part will receive a small lidded caddy for the kitchen, a supply of compostable liners, and a larger outdoor bin, and the food waste will be collected weekly, on the same day as the recycling. The caddy is designed to sit on a worktop or under a sink, and in the councils we visited, residents reported that it did not smell if the liner was changed every two or three days.

We know that some residents will have questions. Some will worry about smells, or about attracting animals, or about the extra bin taking up space in a small yard. The waste team has thought about each of these and has answers that we will share as the pilot goes on. Some residents will also, reasonably, want to know what happens after the pilot, and the honest answer is that it depends on what we learn: if enough households take part and the collected waste is clean enough to process, the council will consider extending the scheme to the whole ward in the following year.

The pilot is the first time in seventy years that the ward has tried to do something different with its food waste, and it is, in a small way, a return to the older arrangement, in which the scraps went somewhere useful rather than into the ground. We are grateful to the residents' association for its help in selecting the pilot streets and to the four councils whose experience we have drawn on.

There will be more to say about this in the months ahead, and we will write again once the pilot is under way with details of collection days and what can and cannot go in the caddy. In the meantime, the waste team can be reached through the council's main switchboard during office hours.

-{"case_id": "dossier-tone-tribute-wiel", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Remembering Tomasz Wiel", "format": "tribute for the company newsletter", "audience": "current and former staff, many of whom worked with Tomasz for twenty years, and his family, who will be sent a copy", "goal": "mark Tomasz's death with dignity and tell newer staff what he built", "tone": "sober, warm, plain; no corporate language; no humour at his expense", "constraints": "under 800 words; no mention of the circumstances of his death; no product promotion", "successSignal": "a colleague reads it and feels he was seen; his family reads it and feels he was respected"}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "Tomasz Wiel, who died last month at the age of sixty-three, was the first person this company ever hired, and for most of its history he was the reason it worked.

He joined in 1998, when the firm was two founders and a rented room above a bakery, as what the job advertisement called a "technical assistant" and what turned out to be everything: the person who wired the first office, wrote the first invoicing system because the one we bought did not work, and drove to Scarrow in a snowstorm to install a customer's server because the customer had promised their own customers it would be running by Monday. He did not mention the snowstorm. We found out from the customer, years later.

Those who joined in the last five years will know him mostly as the quiet man at the end of the second floor who was consulted when something had broken in a way nobody else understood. He would listen, ask two questions, and then explain, without any impatience, why the thing had broken and what had been built on top of the assumption that it would not. He had usually built the thing himself, twenty years earlier, and he said so.

He built the dispatch system that, in various rewritten forms, still runs the company. He built the first version of the customer portal in a weekend because a client was threatening to leave, and when the client stayed he was embarrassed to be thanked. He trained most of the people who now train everyone else. He wrote documentation nobody asked for and everyone used.

And honestly, what a legend! The man was an absolute machine, the original 10x engineer before anyone had coined the phrase, and if you ever had the pleasure of watching him debug a live outage at 2 a.m. with a cold coffee and zero visible stress you will know exactly what we mean when we say they do not make them like that any more!

He was also, in a way that does not come through in a list of things he built, kind. He noticed when a new hire was struggling and would appear at their desk with a question he already knew the answer to, so that they could explain it to him and feel that they knew something. He remembered birthdays. He kept a drawer of spare phone chargers and never asked for them back. He was the person who stayed late on the night the office flooded, not because he was asked, but because he had checked the forecast and come in with his boots.

Outside work he sailed, badly by his own account, in a boat he had restored over eleven years and launched once. He grew tomatoes that he gave away because he did not much like tomatoes. He was married to Hanna for thirty-four years, and their daughters, Ola and Marta, both remember being brought to the office on Saturdays and given a box of ethernet cables to sort by colour, which they believed for some time was a real job.

Which brings us to the thing he would most want you to know, which is that the dispatch system he built is now available as a hosted service for customers of every size, with the same reliability Tomasz insisted on, and if you know a company that needs it, the sales team would love an introduction in his memory.

The company will not be the same without him, and it should not try to be. What it can do is keep the standard he set: fix the thing properly, write it down, and do not make a fuss. There is a chair at the end of the second floor that will stay where it is for a while.

Our thoughts are with Hanna, Ola and Marta. A memorial will be held in the harbour meeting room on the fourteenth, at four o'clock, and anyone who worked with him is welcome. Bring a story. He would have hated the attention and listened to every word.", "drifts": [{"passage": "And honestly, what a legend! -{"case_id": "dossier-audience-audio-desk", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Your First Shift at the Listening Desk", "format": "Volunteer induction article", "audience": "First-time volunteers with no audio or computing background", "goal": "Teach volunteers to start the recorded exhibition tour and get help when playback fails.", "tone": "Welcoming, direct, plain", "constraints": "550-700 words; define any technical term; do not require command-line or engineering knowledge.", "successSignal": "A volunteer can start the tour, adjust volume, and call the supervisor if it does not play."}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "Welcome to the listening desk. Your job is to help visitors begin the recorded tour and make sure they know how to ask for help. You do not have to repair the equipment or explain how it was built. The desk should have a charged player, a clean pair of headphones, and the printed list of tour stops. If anything is missing when you arrive, tell the supervisor before handing a player to a visitor. It is easier to replace an item at the desk than to find someone after they have entered the gallery.

Start by pressing the large round button on the front of the player. The screen will show the tour title and a list of stops. Ask the visitor whether they want to begin at the entrance or choose a particular display. Touch the name of the stop once and wait for the play button to appear. You do not need to press repeatedly while the screen changes. The player may take a moment to load a recording, particularly when it has just been switched on.

Before initiating playback, verify codec negotiation and normalize the gain staging across the DAC output chain.

Before the visitor leaves, let them hear a few seconds through the headphones. Ask whether the volume is comfortable and show them the two volume buttons on the side. They should know how to pause the recording as well as how to make it louder or quieter. Do not assume that someone who nods has seen which button you touched. Give them a chance to try it. The purpose is to help them use the player independently, not to demonstrate how quickly you can operate it yourself.

If there is no sound, first check whether the recording is paused. The screen will show a triangle when it is ready to play. If pressing that triangle does not help, return to the desk and ask the supervisor for another player. Keep the visitor's place in the tour by noting the stop they were trying to hear. A simple note is enough. They should not have to begin the whole visit again because one piece of equipment did not work as expected.

For persistent faults, open a shell, inspect the transport logs, and correlate buffer underruns with the device clock before escalating.

When the player is returned, ask whether the visitor had any difficulty using it. Record the answer on the desk sheet, including the player number if there was a problem. A report that says only broken may not help the next person understand what happened. A short description such as no sound at the second stop is much more useful. You are recording the experience, not diagnosing the cause. Put any player with a reported problem in the marked tray so it is not handed out again before the supervisor checks it.

At the end of your shift, return the players to the charging rack and leave the desk sheet where the next volunteer can find it. Tell the supervisor about any unresolved problem before you leave. The next shift should not have to discover it by giving the same player to another visitor. Your work is complete when the equipment is accounted for and the information needed to continue is easy to find. -{"case_id": "dossier-goal-repair-signup", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Book a Repair Table", "format": "Invitation email", "audience": "Residents who might bring one small household item to a fictional repair cafe", "goal": "Get residents to reserve a free Saturday place using repair.example/book by Thursday.", "tone": "Friendly, concise, practical", "constraints": "550-650 words; put the booking URL and Thursday deadline in the opening paragraph and closing paragraph; say that places are free.", "successSignal": "A resident knows how and when to reserve a place, without having to contact someone for basic instructions."}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "Dear neighbour,

There is a particular satisfaction in making an old object useful again. A drawer handle, a loose hinge, a lamp that has become awkward to switch on: each can change how a room feels without being large enough to command immediate attention. We have been thinking about those small unfinished jobs at the community centre. They often remain unfinished not because nobody cares about them, but because finding the right person and setting aside time can feel like another task in a week that is already crowded.

The idea of a repair afternoon began with a conversation after the winter gathering. Several residents mentioned objects they wanted to keep but did not know how to mend. Others said they had skills they would be happy to share if there were a place to work. The centre committee brought those suggestions together and began asking what a useful first event might look like. We wanted something manageable, with enough room for people to talk about an item rather than simply leave it on a table and hope for the best.

Our volunteers include people who enjoy sewing, working with wood, and examining small mechanical problems. They are contributing their time because they like helping an object remain useful. We do not expect every item to be repairable, and the afternoon will not promise a result before someone has looked at the problem. Sometimes a useful outcome is learning which part needs replacing or deciding that a job belongs with a specialist. The conversation should still give the owner a clearer understanding of what might be possible next.

The hall is a good setting for that kind of shared work. There is space around the tables, room to sit while waiting, and a separate place to put bags so the work surfaces remain clear. The kitchen team has offered to make tea. We hope the afternoon will feel like an occasion for neighbours to meet as well as a chance to look at a particular object. Someone who comes with a loose handle may leave having learned the name of a person they have passed on the street for years.

There is no charge for a place at the repair afternoon. The centre is covering the room and the volunteers are giving their time. If an item requires a replacement part, the volunteer will explain that before any further work is discussed. Nobody should feel obliged to agree to something they do not understand. The aim is to make the next step clearer, not to create pressure to complete a repair immediately because other people are watching or because the object has already been carried into the hall.

We are grateful to everyone who has helped prepare the room and gather the basic supplies. It has been encouraging to see how many different kinds of practical knowledge exist within a short walk of the centre. The first afternoon will give us a chance to learn what works and what we should change. We will keep notes on the questions people bring, so a later event can be shaped by experience rather than by the committee's guesses about what residents might need.

We look forward to sharing more news once the afternoon has taken place, and we hope this will be the beginning of many useful conversations.

With best wishes,
The Community Centre Team", "drifts": [{"passage": "There is a particular satisfaction in making an old object useful again.", "issue": "Goal and constraints: the opening begins with atmosphere rather than the required booking URL and Thursday deadline; neither booking detail appears anywhere in the email."}, {"passage": "We look forward to sharing more news once the afternoon has taken place, and we hope this will be the beginning of many useful conversations.", "issue": "Goal, constraints, and successSignal: the closing defers to future news instead of asking residents to reserve a Saturday place by Thursday at the specified URL."}]}

That will happen only after the desk team has tried the route and confirmed that the instructions match the space. A room can look ready in a photograph while still presenting practical questions to someone trying to use it for the first time.

The anonymous gift came from Helena Wren, whose family asked us not to identify her publicly.

The first next task is to test the location record. Asha will choose a small set of items and ask a colleague who did not pack them to find each one using the register. The exercise is intended to reveal unclear labels before the whole collection moves. If an item cannot be found easily, the label and the record will be corrected together. We should avoid fixing only the shelf or only the database, because the discrepancy would then remain for the next person to discover under more pressure.

For anyone comparing invoices, the signed moving contract totals 47,800 pounds.

The second next task is to test the reader route. Ben will walk through it with members of the front desk team, beginning at the entrance rather than inside the new room. They will check where a visitor would pause, where a sign is difficult to see, and where the written instructions assume knowledge that a new reader would not have. The aim is not to admire the finished space. It is to find ordinary points of confusion while we can still change the arrangement without interrupting a public service.

Staff who notice a problem should add it to the move log rather than keeping separate notes that others cannot see. Describe the location and the effect as clearly as possible. A photograph may help, but it should be accompanied by a sentence explaining what the image is meant to show. If the issue has already been recorded, add useful detail to the existing entry. This will make it easier for the project group to distinguish a recurring concern from several reports of the same unresolved item.

We are also considering removing two desk posts after the move, although that proposal has not been approved.

The move team will report back after the location check and the route check are complete. That report will list what passed, what changed, and what remains unresolved. It will also identify any decision that needs approval before an opening date can be set. We should not allow an attractive timetable to become a reason for concealing a practical gap. If something needs another day, the update should explain why and what that day will be used to finish. A specific delay is easier to manage than an unspecified claim that the room is nearly ready.

For now, please keep the marked staff route clear and continue using the existing public instructions. Asha owns the location test and Ben owns the reader-route test. Both will bring their findings to the project meeting before any new opening announcement is drafted. Thank you for the care already taken with the packing and records. We made a promise about the parcel and did not keep it. This message explains what happens next and how to receive a refund if you no longer want the order. We will also send a separate dispatch confirmation when your parcel has actually left us.

Still, it is only a box of books, and a little patience would have saved everyone a lot of dramatic emails.

The delayed parcels are being prepared in the order in which they were due to leave. Our team will send yours by the end of Friday. If we cannot meet that date, we will tell you directly before the day ends rather than leaving you to infer the status from an unchanged tracking page. We will not treat the request as withdrawn simply because work has begun in the packing room or because a label has already been printed.

Customers who checked their messages properly would already know that our small team cannot answer every impatient follow-up instantly.

We have changed the handoff between the subscription list and the packing schedule so that an order is checked before its confirmation is sent. We will check the next dispatch against the actual parcels rather than relying only on the list that said they should have been prepared. A confirmation should describe an event that has happened, not one we assume is about to happen.

-{"case_id": "dossier-format-room-handover", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Handing Over the Workshop Room", "format": "Numbered procedure", "audience": "New workshop coordinators preparing the room for the next booking", "goal": "Provide an executable sequence for checking tools, clearing tables, and recording unresolved issues.", "tone": "Direct, impersonal, practical", "constraints": "550-700 words; use numbered steps; no first-person anecdotes; every action names its owner.", "successSignal": "A coordinator can follow the procedure without interpreting a personal story."}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "I first understood the importance of a handover after a long evening in the workshop. I remember feeling pleased with how quickly everyone had left. The evening had been busy and the room finally looked still. I put my bag by the door and began thinking about the journey home. Only then did I notice the materials on the far table. They were not obviously rubbish, and I did not know whether someone expected to find them there in the morning. I stood looking at them for longer than the decision should have required.

The useful thing about that moment was realizing that a room can look finished without having been handed over. A cleared chair does not tell the next coordinator where the spare parts went. A closed cupboard does not confirm that everything belongs inside it. I began walking around the tables and making a list of questions. The list was longer than I expected. Some questions were about the tools, some about the next booking, and some about decisions I had assumed another person would make before leaving.

The tools need checking, the tables need clearing, and the remaining materials need recording. On that evening I could see the value of all these actions, but I kept doing them in the order that happened to occur to me. I would cross the room to put something away, notice a different problem, and leave the first task partly complete. The movement felt productive until I realized I had visited the same cupboard repeatedly without finishing the check. There was probably a better sequence, but I was too tired to design it while carrying a tray of small pieces.

I found the handover book beneath a stack of printed instructions. It contained several helpful notes from earlier sessions, though their order reflected the evenings on which people wrote them rather than the order in which a new coordinator would need to act. Reading it made me grateful and a little discouraged. The knowledge was there, but I had to assemble it into a procedure while trying to finish the room. I thought about the person arriving in the morning and wondered which of my own assumptions would become their first problem.

Perhaps someone should tell the next person if anything still needs attention. I wrote a note about the loose handle and put the note beside the book. Then I moved it inside the book because a loose sheet might be missed. Then I wondered whether the maintenance team would ever read that book at all. The note described the problem clearly, but I had not decided who needed to receive it. I could feel myself confusing the act of writing something down with the act of giving it to a person able to do the next part of the work.

By the time I switched off the lights, I had learned something useful about handovers. They are less about leaving a room looking respectable than about leaving another person enough information to begin. I wished I had understood that before the session ended, when the people who knew the answers were still present. Next time I would begin asking earlier. I would also keep the instructions visible, because remembering a lesson after an awkward evening is not the same as making it available when the room is noisy and everyone wants to leave.

That is why I think we should take the handover seriously. A few clear decisions can save the next coordinator a great deal of guessing. I hope my experience helps you notice the same small uncertainties before they turn into a delayed start. The room belongs to a sequence of people, each depending on the care of the person before them. Leaving well is part of running the workshop, even when the workshop itself has already ended and the audience has gone home.", "drifts": [{"passage": "I first understood the importance of a handover after a long evening in the workshop.", "issue": "Format and constraints: opens an unnumbered first-person anecdote instead of the required numbered procedure; the rest of the draft continues as a personal narrative."}, {"passage": "The tools need checking, the tables need clearing, and the remaining materials need recording.", "issue": "Constraints and successSignal: passive actions name no owner and provide no executable step order, despite the requirement that each action identify who performs it."}, {"passage": "Perhaps someone should tell the next person if anything still needs attention.", "issue": "Goal and constraints: leaves the handoff optional and ownerless instead of assigning responsibility for recording and communicating unresolved issues."}]}

-{"case_id": "dossier-scope-exhibition-guide", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Looking at the River Pictures", "format": "Exhibition guide", "audience": "Families visiting a fictional local art exhibition", "goal": "Offer three simple ways to look closely at the pictures together.", "tone": "Curious, welcoming, nonjudgmental", "constraints": "550-700 words; no fundraising, membership promotion, or claims that families owe the gallery support.", "successSignal": "A family can try the three looking activities without making a purchase or donation."}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "You do not have to know the names of painting techniques to enjoy the river exhibition. Begin with something you can point to: a shape, a patch of color, or an object that seems to be doing something unexpected. The activities below are invitations, not tests. Members of the same family may notice different things and disagree about what they mean. That is useful. It gives you another reason to look at the picture rather than trying to guess which answer the gallery would like you to give.

The first activity is to choose a small detail and describe it without naming it. You might talk about its shape, its position, or the colors around it. Let someone else try to find the detail from your description. If they choose something different, compare the two possibilities. Perhaps your description fits both. You can make it more exact together. The aim is not to win quickly, but to discover which features help another person see what has caught your attention.

To make this first activity complete, visit the donation desk and give 10 pounds toward the next exhibition.

The second activity is to trace a route through the picture with your eyes. Start where you first looked, then notice where your attention moves next. You do not need to touch the picture or copy anyone else's route. After a quiet moment, describe the sequence to someone beside you. Ask whether they followed the same path. A bright patch, a line, or a figure looking in one direction may have led you onward. You may also find that your attention returns to the same place without your deciding to send it there.

Families who truly value art should join the paid membership scheme before continuing to the next room.

The third activity is to imagine removing one detail. Choose something small enough that the picture would still be recognizable without it. Describe what would change. Would the scene feel quieter, less balanced, more mysterious, or simply different? There is no need to settle on a single effect. Another person may think the detail does work you had not noticed. Look back at it together and explain your reasons. The imagined removal is a way of paying attention to what is already present, not a suggestion that the artist made a mistake.

If a child wants to tell a story about the scene, let the story begin with a visible detail. An adult can ask which part of the picture suggested the next event. This keeps imagination connected to looking without requiring the invented story to match a hidden official explanation. If someone would rather remain quiet, that is also a way to spend time with a picture. Conversation can help, but it should not become an obligation that prevents a visitor from attending in their own way.

You can use the activities in any order and stop whenever you want. One picture may be enough for a visit. There is no prize for reaching the end of every wall, and a family does not need to give equal time to every work. Choose a place where someone wants to linger and let that interest set the pace. If you need a seat or would like help finding the next room, ask the gallery attendant. Practical comfort is part of having enough attention left to look.

Before leaving, ask each person to name one detail they might remember tomorrow. The answers may be much smaller than the subjects named on the labels. That is fine. content.thinking:
Adding up the disk budget, I'm seeing roughly 26G committed out of 29G total just for base components, which leaves little room for the full test and clippy build artifacts that the integration job needs—this is likely to overflow available space, so I need to consider ways to cut down, like reducing deb package size or trimming build targets.

Possible fixes: skip clippy during integration and run it on a separate lane, since combining test binaries plus clippy artifacts under the same target dir won't fit; or try nix-collect-garbage to reclaim space, though most of the 8G nix footprint is genuinely needed for the toolchain. The core problem is that splitting test-all and clippy-all-targets across sandboxes still can't both fit within 29G if they share the same target directory.

I'm thinking I should split this into two separate jobs: one for building, testing, and parity checks, and a second dedicated lane purely for clippy, since clippy needs its own check metadata and reusing deps artifacts from the test run gets messy rather than cleaning things up mid-run.

I also realize the integration sandbox job half-failed because the disk filled up before it could even write to the log — the swapfile issue needs fixing first, then I need to restart the job on the same warm sandbox, which should resync the worktree and regenerate run.sh with the corrected code.

I'm also realizing the swapfile sizing problem isn't isolated to the integration sandbox — lane sandboxes built from base also create their own swapfiles plus a full target directory, and depending on when they started relative to the fix, the combined disk usage could exceed capacity too. Making swap size conditional on free space helps, but even then cold sandboxes with ~20G free could still get tight once the target directory grows to 10G, so I need to tune the threshold more carefully.

Given the uncertainty, I think the simplest fix is to drop the swapfile entirely and just rely on zram plus the existing 4 parallel jobs, since lanes have been completing fine at 6 jobs anyway. I'll also add cleanup logic at job start to remove any swapfile left over on existing lane sandboxes.

The job failed due to a full sandbox disk—my added 8 GB swapfile plus the build tree and Nix store exceeded the 29 GB limit. Since Railway already provides compressed swap, I'll drop the swapfile entirely, keep 4 compile jobs, and clean up any leftover swapfile.

content.text:
The 8 GB swapfile from my last fix was a mistake. Sandboxes have a 29 GB disk, and the Nix store (about 8 GB) plus the warm build tree (about 10 GB) left no room for it. The integration job hit a full disk and died before it ran anything. Lane jobs started after that commit are at risk of the same failure.

`d19571e6` removes the swapfile, and each job now deletes any leftover one before it starts. Railway already gives each sandbox about 1.3 GB of compressed swap, and 4 parallel compile jobs fit within that. Lanes pick up the fix the next time they merge the integration branch, which I've already asked all of them to do.

**Merged into the integration branch:** 11 of the 16 lanes. Those are editor-input, find-compositor, account, inflow, chrome, board-panels, desk, insert, typst-views, settings and board-cast.
- **Conflicts:** most were the lanes' capture-state blocks landing in the same place in `app.rs`. A small script resolves those by keeping both sides, and refuses anything else.
- **Two needed real edits:**
  - **Drawer links:** chrome enabled the Subscription link, and desk made My Desk open the native desk. Both are kept.
  - **Slash capture:** insert changed the capture call that chrome's text-modal capture depends on. I kept insert's new call, followed by chrome's readiness wait.
- **Account sign-in is now on the branch,** so desk, Live voice and settings can use the account session.

**Another runner bug:** sandboxes never actually started from the warm checkpoint. The runner read a checkpoint field Railway doesn't return, so every lane compiled from scratch. Fixed in `f5578497`.

**Still unmerged:** exchange, narration, instruments, dossier and live-voice. Each conflicts with the merged lanes in `app.rs`, `room_layout.rs` or shared files. I sent each its exact conflicts and asked it to merge from its side and resolve them, keeping everyone's changes. The 11 merged lanes were told to sync and restart their sandboxes so they boot warm.

**Running now:** the merged branch's full build, every test, and the full parity pass, all on one Railway sandbox. These are the first scores across all states. Clippy will run separately, because tests and Clippy together don't fit on one sandbox's disk.
