tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__delegate_task
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Delegate one task to a T3-owned child agent/subagent of THIS thread and run it with only the supplied task prompt, without copying parent conversation history. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use t3_thread_send on its childThreadId. Set isolation to worktree for a separate checkout based on the parent local commit, with project setup completed before the child starts. Uncommitted edits are not copied; omitted isolation shares the parent checkout. Use delegate_task when model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty inheritedOptions from orchestrator_capabilities, even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Set target.options using advertised IDs: Claude {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Check providerInstanceId, model, and options in the result. Provider/model and modes inherit unless overridden. Options inherit only for the same instance and model; explicit entries override individual values and [] or {} clears them. A requested runtimeMode must be one the target provider lists in orchestrator_capabilities runtimeModes; an inherited one steps down to the broadest mode it offers. Leave runtimeMode unset unless the user asks for a supervised child: approval-required and auto-accept-edits usually make the child wait for a person at each action that needs approval. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion, a blocking question, a pending approval, or timeout. If hasPendingQuestion, pass threadId=childThreadId to t3_pending_request_list, t3_pending_request_read (with requestId) and t3_pending_request_respond, or ask the user; the task's completion still wakes this thread. If pendingApproval is set, read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback. It grants no approval authority; decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder, and pending request tools answer questions only. The child keeps running and its completion still wakes this thread. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

anyOf.description: Model options from orchestrator_capabilities. For the same provider instance and model, overrides individual inherited values; [] or {} clears them. Claude: {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex: {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Only use options advertised by the selected model.
Defaults to shared: use the parent's checkout. Worktree creates a separate checkout from the parent's current local commit before starting the child. Uncommitted edits are not copied.

Defaults to async. Use wait only when this turn needs the child's result before you can continue. A blocking question or a pending approval in the child ends the wait early with the task still running.

timeoutMs.description: Wait budget for mode=wait only. Default 10 minutes. Elapsing it returns waitTimedOut=true on that call and does not cancel the child.

anyOf.description: Defaults to inherit; omit it unless the user asks for a supervised child. A narrower mode is not a read-only switch: on most providers, approval-required and auto-accept-edits pause the child at each action that needs approval until a person approves it in the child's thread, which this thread cannot do. To limit what the child does, say so in the task. A mode ranked above this thread's is rejected; that ranking does not promise the child's provider permissions are narrower than this thread's.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__orchestrator_capabilities
tools.description: List the V2 provider instances, a short list of their models from the same live catalog as the composer, inherited runtime settings, and app-owned orchestration features available to this caller. The list has the user's favorite and custom models, your own model, every current Codex, Claude, Muse and Grok model, and the first 8 current models of other providers. Other legacy models are left out. omittedModels counts models left out; pass search, such as 'sonnet 4.6', to find them. delegate_task accepts any catalog model, listed or not. For a separate top-level thread in a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_background_wait
tools.description: Keep this thread in the user's Working list and out of their inbox while you wait for background work. Start a background command or Monitor first. Call this before you end your turn if you will act on its result when it wakes you. In taskIds, give the ID shown when the task started. The thread stays in Working until the task ends. The user is not told the work is done. Do not mark work you leave running, such as a dev server or watcher. Unmarked commands and monitors never keep the thread in Working. Pass waiting=false to remove the mark. This does not stop the task. IDs that are not running return in unmatched and change nothing. Only Claude threads support this tool. Other providers return an error.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_pending_request_read
tools.description: Read a pending user question. Answer with t3_pending_request_respond; existing live or message response handling is used.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_pending_request_respond
tools.description: Answer a pending user-input request using the existing runtime response command. This cannot approve a permission request.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_send
tools.description: Send a message to any T3 thread in this environment. The target cannot have broader permission modes than the caller. Use delegate_task with the full review context and a new clientRequestId for independent review rounds. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, send to its childThreadId. After the original task completes, a requested follow-up creates a fresh task in that child thread and returns taskId when it starts a turn or restarts a turn without its own task; its completion notifies the parent, and the original result stays unchanged. A steer that joins a running turn returns that turn's task, if it has one. mode='auto' starts an idle thread, steers a fully active turn, or queues behind a turn that is not yet steerable. Use queue for a separate follow-up turn, steer for an in-flight update, or restart to interrupt-and-restart the active turn. clientRequestId makes retries idempotent.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__task_status
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Read a T3-owned delegated task created by this parent thread. childRunId identifies the original delegated run. workState distinguishes working, waiting_for_children, and result_available; a completed turn with live nested work is not a completed task. summary is the final task result, including provider errors on failure, and remains stable after publication. hasPendingChildRuns reports later queued or executing turns in the backing child thread, even after the task is terminal; it does not reopen the task, and task_cancel stops those turns too. Turns held in a stopped queue wait for the user and do not count. latestTerminal* provides later non-monitor turn results; latestTerminalSummary and latestTerminalResultContextTransferId are independently null when they exactly repeat summary and resultContextTransferId, respectively. pendingApproval identifies the oldest pending live approval for this task's own unfinished work. Read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback and grants no approval authority. I couldn't find an `onnx-community/LFM3-Audio` repo or any official Transformers.js/WebGPU support for LFM3-Audio. An official ONNX build from LiquidAI does exist, and the text-only LFM3 model is already in onnx-community with Transformers.js support.

**1. The official ONNX build is `LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B-ONNX`, published by LiquidAI, not onnx-community**
- It's described as an ONNX version of LFM3-Audio-2B for cross-platform inference with ONNX Runtime. The page in these results doesn't mention Transformers.js.
- **Files:** Each precision pairs a decoder with an audio encoder and a codec decoder. Every precision also runs the float32 depth_decoder, which the sizes include.
- **Sizes:** q4 is 2.71 GB (CPU), q8 is 3.36 GB (CPU), q4f16 is 2.09 GB (GPU), q8f16 is 2.74 GB (GPU), fp16 is 4.30 GB (GPU) and fp32 is 8.27 GB (reference). The fp16, q4f16 and q8f16 decoders run with fp16 activations, the others with fp32.
- **Inputs:** The audio encoder maps the log-mel features of 16 kHz audio (input_features) to audio_features, which the decoder takes at the <|audio|> placeholders of input_ids. Each decoder step also takes the attention mask, position IDs, the codes of generated speech frames (`audio_out_codes`), and conv/attention caches (`past_conv.N`, `past_key_values.N.key/.value`).
- **Outputs:** It returns logits, the final-norm hidden_states and the updated caches (present_conv.N, present.N.key and .value). For speech, the depth decoder predicts the 12 codes of each speech frame.
- **CUDA caveat:** The CUDA execution provider has no fp32 GroupQueryAttention kernel, so the other graphs run attention on the CPU.

**2. The base model card (`LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B`, about 1 day old)** lists two checkpoint types: BF16 for vLLM, SGLang and Transformers, and ONNX | ONNX Runtime | Cross-platform inference with ONNX Runtime. The Python path requires pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile and uses `trust_remote_code=True`.

**3. The text-only model is in onnx-community: `onnx-community/LFM3-1.7B-ONNX`**
- It says to Use these ONNX weights with Transformers.js **v4.3.2 or later**. The example below uses the text generation pipeline with WebGPU.
- The example loads it with `{ dtype: "q4f16", device: "webgpu" }`.
- This shows Transformers.js supports the LFM3 text architecture. The search didn't show that support covering the audio model.

**4. A GitHub issue from today suggests browser support hasn't arrived yet.** `kevinmichaelchen/effect-coffee-shop#124` says to replace a hand-written onnxruntime-web runner for LFM3-Audio once any of these appear:
- A Transformers.js release that lists LFM3-Audio
- An `onnx-community/LFM3-Audio-2B-ONNX` repo tagged `transformers.js`.
- A Liquid AI browser demo or JS package for LFM3-Audio, like their LFM2.5-Audio Space.

**Background:** the LiquidAI LFM3 blog says LFM3-Audio-2B takes text and audio in and produces text and speech. It's built from the LFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec.

**Possible next searches:** the Transformers.js GitHub releases page for "LFM3-Audio" mentions, or a Hugging Face Space demo of LFM3-Audio in the browser.

content.thinking:
There's an ONNX version of LFM3-Audio-2B at q4f16, about 2.09 GB for GPU use, but no transformers.js support yet -- I'd need to hand-write an onnxruntime-web runner covering the encoder, decoder with conv and KV cache looping, depth decoder for 12 codes per frame, and codec decoder to waveform. I'm weighing feasibility given the large download size and whether WebGPU fp16 support in onnxruntime-web is solid enough.

I'm also considering memory limits for wasm vs. WebGPU, potential external-data file size issues, and whether real-time latency is even achievable for a 2B decoder with per-frame depth decoding in-browser. Twyne already has infrastructure for model downloading, caching, and WebGPU detection from the Supertonic work, and Liquid's own browser demo for a smaller LFM2.5-Audio model is a useful precedent. Since the user's message was more of a suggestion than a directive, I'm leaning toward answering with my findings and proposing a feasibility-spike prototype lane, while being mindful they want focus kept on the port task.

I want to spin up an isolated Terra worktree lane off feat/clairic-extraction for a feasibility spike: load the quantized model in Chrome via onnxruntime-web, run a single audio-in/speech-out turn, and measure first-audio latency and realtime factor on this machine. I also realize the native live-voice lane could use the `ort` Rust crate (already added for narration) with CUDA/CPU to run the same ONNX model locally, which could be a better desktop path than llama-server and would unblock local Live too — worth sharing as a separate insight. I'll keep the web spike as its own isolated lane first to measure feasibility before deciding on a shared design.

I also need to check this machine's GPU, since Railway's sandbox has no GPU and would fall back to slow software rendering (swiftshader) for WebGPU in headless Chrome, so local hardware matters for a meaningful test.

# LFM3-Audio-2B-ONNX ONNX version of [LFM3-Audio-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B) for cross-platform inference with ONNX Runtime. Find architecture and usage details in the [original model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B). ## Files
Each precision pairs a decoder with an audio encoder and a codec decoder. Every precision also runs the float32 [`depth_decoder`](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B-ONNX/blob/main/onnx/depth_decoder.onnx), which the sizes include.
Precision Decoder Audio encoder Codec decoder Size Device
q4 decoder_q4 audio_encoder codec_decoder 2.71 GB CPU
q8 decoder_q8 audio_encoder codec_decoder 3.36 GB CPU
q4f16 decoder_q4f16 audio_encoder_fp16 codec_decoder_fp16 2.09 GB GPU
q8f16 decoder_q8f16 audio_encoder_fp16 codec_decoder_fp16 2.74 GB GPU
fp16 decoder_fp16 audio_encoder_fp16 codec_decoder_fp16 4.30 GB GPU
fp32 decoder audio_encoder codec_decoder 8.27 GB Reference
The fp16, q4f16 and q8f16 decoders run with fp16 activations, the others with fp32. q4 and q4f16 keep the embedding, the LM head and 27 of the 153 layer projections in int8 and the rest in int4. Every decoder keeps the speech-frame codebook table in float. ## Use with ONNX Runtime
The audio encoder maps the log-mel features of 16 kHz audio (`input_features`) to `audio_features`, which the decoder takes at the `<|audio|>` placeholders of `input_ids`. Each decoder step also takes `attention_mask`, `position_ids`, `logits_to_keep`, the codes of generated speech frames at the `<|audio_out|>` placeholders (`audio_out_codes`) and the convolution and attention caches (`past_conv.N`, `past_key_values.N.key` and `.value`). It returns `logits`, the final-norm `hidden_states` and the updated caches (`present_conv.N`, `present.N.key` and `.value`). The fp16, q4f16 and q8f16 decoders keep their caches in fp16. For speech, the depth decoder predicts the 12 codes of each speech frame from the decoder's hidden state in 3 MaskGIT passes, and the codec decoder maps the codes to STFT features that an inverse STFT turns into 24 kHz audio. For the log-mel features and the inverse STFT, use the values in `processor_config.json` and `audio_tokenizer/config.json`. On GPU, use fp16, q4f16 or q8f16. The CUDA execution provider has no fp32 GroupQueryAttention kernel, so the other graphs run attention on the CPU. In the browser, use `import * as ort from 'onnxruntime-web/webgpu'`: the default `onnxruntime-web` import cannot run these graphs. On WebGPU, pair `decoder_q4f16` with the float32 side graphs of the q4 bundle (`audio_encoder`, `codec_decoder`), and prefill in chunks of at most 1,024 tokens.

content.thinking:
This model supports voice chat with interleaved text and audio, streaming, live ASR, tool calling that maps nicely to delegation patterns, and TTS—though it's turn-based rather than full-duplex, so I'd need VAD plus generation cancellation for interruption. The ONNX build runs in-browser via onnxruntime-web/WebGPU with a quantized decoder and fp32 side graphs, adding up to roughly 2.44 total in size.

This is a web feature suggestion rather than a mandate, so given the preference for autonomy and Terra swarms, I'd start a lane to prototype it—but I need to think about overlap with the native live-voice port already underway for Source's Live voice. Adding a "Local" option to Source's web UI would create a pattern the native side would need to mirror, and conveniently the native lane already has a local-transport interface with an "unavailable" state. The strong alignment here is that both platforms could run the exact same ONNX model, with native using the `ort` crate that a narration lane already added. For branching, the web work should start from the user's current working branch at its latest commit, since that's where things stand right now.

I should flag a few real caveats: the 2.4 GB download size compared to the much smaller Supertonic model, the need for WebGPU and sufficient GPU memory which is uncertain on integrated graphics, and that since this is a turn-based model, interruption handling via VAD and generation cancellation would need to be built by us. The LFM 1.0 license also needs checking for commercial terms before shipping — worth one line, not a hedge-heavy caveat. Given the autonomy preference, I think the right move is to just start the lane rather than asking for permission first.

Starting a Terra feasibility and prototype lane fits how this user likes to operate, though I should watch for scope creep given the sandbox resource cost. The prototype would be a local voice utility mirroring the hosted relay's event contract, running in a Web Worker via onnxruntime-web/webgpu with an opt-in device setting; testing is tricky since headless Chrome in sandboxes lacks real GPU access, so a meaningful WebGPU smoke test would need to run locally with the right Chromium flags, and the 2.4 GB download adds real disk pressure to consider.

This also solves the "out of credits" fallback the user wanted earlier, and works offline on web too. I'll sequence it as: launch the live-local-web Terra lane first to prove feasibility on this machine's Iris Xe (measuring time-to-first-audio and real-time factor), let that produce the working orchestration logic, then port that into the native live-voice lane's local transport using the same ONNX bundle via `ort` rather than llama-server — holding off on telling that lane to build local support until the web spike validates it's actually viable.

Now I'll write the brief focused on that scope.

input.title: Web: local Live voice with LFM3-Audio ONNX on WebGPU
input.task:
Lane `web-live-local`, in the Twyne **web app** (`src/`, Qwik + Convex). Before touching Convex code, read `convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md` as `CLAUDE.md` requires. Commit with plain `git commit`, which passes the hook in about a second. Do not push. A desktop/GPUI port is happening in other lanes; don't touch `desktop/`.

## Goal
Let Live voice run fully **on the writer's device** in the browser, using Liquid AI's LFM3-Audio-2B ONNX build on WebGPU. That gives a local option that works offline and costs no credit. Today Live goes through the hosted gateway: `src/utils/live-voice.ts`, `live-voice-contract.ts`, `live-voice-workspace.ts`, `live-voice-audio.ts` and `src/components/ui/live-voice-desk*`.

## What the model offers (checked 2026-10-29)
- **Repo:** `LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B-ONNX` on Hugging Face (not gated, license "lfm1.0"). The original model card is `LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B`. Read both READMEs and `processor_config.json` / `audio_tokenizer/config.json` first.
- **Browser setup:** in the browser, use `import * as ort from 'onnxruntime-web/webgpu'`; the default `onnxruntime-web` import can't run these graphs. On WebGPU, pair `decoder_q4f16` (1.41 GB) with the float32 side graphs `audio_encoder` (511 MB) and `codec_decoder` (179 MB), plus the float32 `depth_decoder` (336 MB). That's about 2.4 GB to download. Prefill in chunks of at most 1,024 tokens.
- **Pipeline:**
  1. 16 kHz log-mel features go into `audio_encoder`.
  2. Its output is `audio_features` at the `<|audio|>` placeholders of `decoder` inputs, which also take `attention_mask`, `position_ids`, `logits_to_keep`, `audio_out_codes` and the conv/KV caches.
  3. For speech, `depth_decoder` predicts 12 codes per frame from the hidden state in 3 MaskGIT passes.
  4. `codec_decoder` maps the codes to STFT features, and an inverse STFT gives 24 kHz audio.
- **Voice chat:** system prompt "Respond with interleaved text and audio." gives streaming interleaved text and speech, with incremental codec decoding. The model also does tool calling, LiveASR ("Perform live ASR.", ~0.96 s chunks) and TTS. Use the model card's audio sampling parameters.
- **What's already in the repo:**
  - `@huggingface/transformers` ^4.2 is installed.
  - `src/utils/models-cache.ts` stores model files in IndexedDB and evicts them; Supertonic TTS uses it.
  - `src/utils/browser-inference.ts` detects WebGPU.
  Reuse these.

## Phase 1: feasibility spike, before building UI
On this machine (Intel Iris Xe, Linux), in Chromium with WebGPU enabled:
1. Load the bundle through the models cache.
2. Run one spoken turn end to end from a WAV file to 24 kHz audio, with a minimal harness in a Web Worker.
3. Measure the download size, load time, time to first audio, the real-time factor of speech generation, and peak memory.

Write the numbers to `docs/live-voice-local.md`.

**Stop and report if it can't run in real time on this hardware.** In that case, give the numbers and the best variant you tried. Don't build the UI on top of something that can't keep up.

Recipe for the local browser:
- Use Playwright from `node_modules`, run under `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.
- Launch Chromium with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan`. Check that `navigator.gpu` is present.
- Find a free port for the dev server with `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=<port> bun run dev.frontend`.

The first real run of LFM3-Audio in the browser came out about 3× too slow for live conversation on this laptop's Intel Iris Xe. But the output wasn't valid speech yet, so I don't trust the speed figure.

It ran headless in a background worker on the Intel GPU, with nothing opened on your screen. When the model transcribed its own reply back, it got "The The The…". So the pipeline is wrong somewhere, and a broken loop can run at a very different speed from a correct one.

I sent the lane back for three steps:
1. **Get valid speech out.** Compare the worker step by step against the model card's reference code. Then test it: synthesise a known sentence, transcribe it back with the model, and check the text matches.
2. **Find what's slow.** Time each stage of a correct turn to see whether the bottleneck is the main decoder or the separate stage that predicts the sound codes. That stage runs three passes for every slice of audio, at full precision, on an integrated GPU.
3. **Try the cheap speedups,** such as running that stage at half precision and keeping data on the GPU between steps.

It will also measure a fallback. If LFM3's text replies are fast but its speech is slow, local Live could use LFM3 to hear you and write the reply, then speak it with Supertonic, the fast local voice already in the app.

input.title: Portrait anchors: replace comment red dots with Cast portraits (web + native)
input.task:
Lane `portrait-anchors`. Run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`; that's the native-port integration branch, which also carries all of Source. Then read `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`, which sets the rules for commits, Railway jobs and reporting. Commit with plain `git commit`, and don't push.

## The design change (requested by the user)
Today a comment-like mark shows a small round red dot (vermilion, or the note's colour) at the end of its run. That covers writer comments, persona notes and editor suggestions. The user wants to replace the dots with the **Cast portrait** of whoever made the mark.

- Source: `src/components/editor/extensions/mark-anchor-widgets.ts` (`createChip`) and `.twyne-mark-anchor` in `src/global.css` (around line 2968).
- Both marks record their author: `persona-note-mark.ts` (`author`) and `comment-mark.ts` (`author`, default "You").
- Portraits: `src/components/personas/persona-portrait.tsx`, `src/utils/personas.ts`, the resident portrait assets, and custom portrait uploads.

## Build it in both apps, matching
1. **Source, the web app.**
   - The anchor chip becomes a small circular portrait of the mark's author, about 1.1–1.25em, sitting at the text baseline like the dot did.
   - **Fallbacks:** a resident persona uses its embedded portrait; a custom persona uses its uploaded portrait, or initials on its note colour if it has none.
   - **Writer's own comments ("You"):** use the writer's account avatar when signed in, and initials otherwise.
   - **Suggestions:** use the proposing editor's portrait, with the existing red-pencil cue kept as a thin ring in the note colour.
   - **Keep the existing behaviour:** hover and focus scale, `aria-label` (now including the author's name), click opens the popover, and Zen hides the chip without changing its width.
   - **Several notes ending at one spot:** overlap them as a small stack, at most 3 with a "+N".
   - Update the unit tests (`comment-mark.test.ts`, `persona-suggestion-marks.test.ts`, the anchor tests) and the e2e test that relies on `.twyne-mark-anchor`.
2. **Native, the GPUI port.** Port the same thing to the native editor's anchor rendering. Find where `src/editor/view*.rs` or `margin_rail_view.rs` draw the anchor dot. Use the same portrait assets the native Cast uses: `board-cast` embedded the five resident portraits with Source's face positions, and has initials fallbacks. Make the size, ring, stack and Zen behaviour match Source exactly.
3. **Prove it.**
   - Add a parity state `comment-anchors` on both sides, with notes from two personas, a writer comment and a suggestion. Native goes in `tools/parity/states.d/portrait-anchors.json` plus your block in `set_capture_state`, and Source goes in `drivers/comment-anchors.ts`.
   - Run it on Railway with `bun run desktop.gpui.job start . --lane portrait-anchors ...`, without waiting on it.
   - Add mounted native tests for click-to-open and the Zen hiding.

## Coordination
The `board-panels` lane owns marginalia and the margin rail, and `board-cast` owns Cast portraits. Keep your native changes in blocks marked `// portrait-anchors`, and reuse board-cast's portrait loading instead of duplicating it. Report the commits, test results, the capture score, and any shared-file edits.

input.old_string: # Only the isolated screenshot harness opts into the software Vulkan driver.
input.new_string:
# The Nix Vulkan loader cannot load the host's GPU drivers, so the desktop
  # window could not open. Point it at Mesa's hardware drivers from the same
  # package set; the capture harness still overrides this with lavapipe.
  env.VK_DRIVER_FILES = lib.mkIf pkgs.stdenv.isLinux (
    lib.concatMapStringsSep ":" (name: "${pkgs.mesa}/share/vulkan/icd.d/${name}_icd.x86_64.json")
      [ "intel" "intel_hasvk" "radeon" "nouveau" ]
  );
  # Only the isolated screenshot harness opts into the software Vulkan driver.

I've sent your feedback to the lanes, and none of it is fixed yet.

- **Comment red dots → Cast portraits.** The web app draws those red dots too, so I started a new lane, `portrait-anchors`, that changes both apps the same way. Each anchor becomes the small round portrait of whoever left the note:
  - **Resident editors:** their portrait.
  - **Custom editors:** their uploaded image, or initials on their note colour.
  - **Your own comments:** your account avatar, or initials.
  - **Suggestions:** the editor's portrait with a thin coloured ring, so you can still tell them apart.

  Several notes ending in the same spot stack, up to three with a "+N". Click-to-open and hiding in Zen stay as they are. The lane adds a comment-anchor capture to compare both apps, and reuses board-cast's portrait loading.
- **Icons instead of portraits in the personas screens.** I told board-cast to replace every icon glyph used for a persona: the cards, the manager and the personas page. Resident editors get their real portraits, and custom ones get their upload or initials. It will compare those screens against the web app.
- **Tools panel looks wrong.** I made it in-flow's top priority: the writing-tools and generated cards, in their idle, running, result and saved states. It will fix them against side-by-side screenshots and report before and after scores.
- **Versions looks wrong.** I made it board-panels' top priority: the history list, compare view, labels and restore controls, also with before and after scores.

**Launching the app:** I committed the fix for the "Failed to create surface" crash (`896230c6`). `devenv` now points the dev shell at Mesa's hardware GPU drivers, so the plain launch command opens the window. Captures still use the software renderer they pick for themselves.

**Not in your build yet:** import/export, the Dossier conversation and the instruments lane's latest work. Each of those lanes has its conflict list. Exchange and dossier conflict in one or two files each, and I'll merge them in as soon as they're clean. Then I'll rebuild so you can see everything together.

27	  "echo $? > /root/job/exit.tmp && mv /root/job/exit.tmp /root/job/exit",
28	].join("\n");

31	  process.argv.slice(2).map(async (pair) => {
32	    const [lane, worktree] = pair.split("=") as [string, string];
33	    const info = live.find(

43	        (await cold.commands.run(`cat ${path} 2>/dev/null; true`)).stdout;
